terms.meaning: How much the total Gibbs energy changes per mole of an element added, for a small addition at fixed T, p and fixed amounts of the other elements. Written with an element subscript, for example μA or μNi.
terms.elsewhere: In step 06, “μ phase” (MU_PHASE) is the name of a Ni–Nb phase, not a chemical potential.

terms.meaning: An ordered Ni–Nb phase with ideal formula Nb₇Ni₆ and five sublattices in ratio 2:2:2:6:1 (13 atoms per formula unit).
terms.elsewhere: μ with an element subscript (μA, μNi) is a chemical potential, as in steps 02–04.

terms.meaning: An energy in J/mol boundary sites. The boundary function is gs = gb + δθ (+ η, which is zero in step 04’s main model), so a negative δ lowers the energy of B on boundary sites and attracts B to the boundary.
terms.elsewhere: In step 06, “δ phase” (DELTA) is the name of a Ni–Nb phase.

terms.meaning: An ordered Ni–Nb phase with ideal formula NbNi₃ and three sublattices in ratio 1:1:2 (4 atoms per formula unit).
terms.elsewhere: δ on its own is the boundary preference energy of step 04.

terms.meaning: Gibbs energy per mole of formula units. One formula unit of the δ phase holds 4 atoms, one of the μ phase 13.
terms.elsewhere: G alone is the Gibbs energy of a whole sample in J; GM is per mole of atoms.

terms.meaning: Gibbs energy per mole of atoms, in J/mol (pycalphad’s name). It is already per atom: do not divide it again.
terms.elsewhere: G_formula is per mole of formula units.

terms.meaning: Molar Gibbs energy of the bulk ALPHA phase, J/mol atoms. The b stands for bulk.
terms.elsewhere: gs is the boundary function; the b in gb and xb never means “boundary”.

terms.meaning: Energy of the boundary sites as a function of their B occupancy θ: gs(θ) = gb(θ) + δθ + η, in J/mol boundary sites (η = 0 in step 04’s main model).
terms.elsewhere: gb is the bulk curve from step 02.

terms.meaning: B fraction of the bulk sites. The b stands for bulk.
terms.elsewhere: θ is the B fraction of the boundary sites; z is the overall fraction of a whole sample.

terms.meaning: A constant energy of a boundary state, in J/mol boundary sites, added whatever the occupancy. The main step 04 model has η = 0.
terms.elsewhere: Only the extension compares a state with η = 2000 J/mol boundary sites.

terms.meaning: Database names for crystal structures: face-centred cubic, body-centred cubic and hexagonal close-packed. A1, A2 and A3 are the traditional structure codes. Cu and Ni are both FCC.
pycalphad’s word for one coexisting phase in an equilibrium result. Two vertices can carry the same phase name with different compositions.

An extra Gibbs-energy term for phases that order magnetically, like ferromagnetic Ni. It lowers the energy most at low temperature, shrinks as the Curie temperature is approached (where its heat capacity peaks), keeps a small tail above it, and is already part of the total G.
The temperature below which a material is ferromagnetic. For pure Ni it is about 630 K; in the alloy model it changes with composition.

A composition range in which one phase model (one structure) describes two coexisting phases of different composition, for example two FCC phases in Cu–Ni at low temperature. Databases and pycalphad keep the same phase name for both.
The lens-shaped two-phase region between the liquidus (above it, all liquid) and the solidus (below it, all solid) in a diagram like Cu–Ni. Inside it, liquid and FCC coexist.
B fraction of the whole sample, whatever phases it splits into. Fixed by the amounts of A and B you put in.
terms.elsewhere: x is the B fraction inside one phase or region.

terms.meaning: A Ni–Nb phase with a fixed composition in step 06's database, exactly one Nb in nine atoms: a line compound.

modules.title: Start here · energies, terms and CALPHAD

blocks.text: In plain words: Every calculation in this course asks one question: which state has the lowest energy under the conditions you hold fixed? This step collects the energies, words and symbols you will meet, so you can come back whenever a term looks unfamiliar. Picture: a ladder of energies, U, H, F and G, each fitting different conditions.

Cards you may need: [[card#conditions-potential|conditions and potential]], [[card#why-min-g|why minimise G]], [[card#work-sign|the sign of work]], [[card#reversible|reversible transfer]], [[card#isolated-closed-open|isolated, closed or open]].

Why CALPHAD? Imagine heating a sealed metal specimen. Which phases can it contain at equilibrium, and how much of each? CALPHAD (CALculation of PHAse Diagrams) answers this from a Gibbs-energy model for every candidate phase. A database stores those models and their parameters. A calculation program evaluates them and searches for the combination of phases with the lowest total Gibbs energy that still contains the right amount of each element. Loading a database alone does not give you the equilibrium.

A phase diagram maps the answer: for each temperature and composition it shows which phases are present. You will read real ones for Cu–Ni and Ni–Nb in steps 05 and 06. Such calculations are only as good as their inputs: model parameters are chosen to match experiments and other calculations, so agreement with those same data is not an independent test. Equilibrium also says nothing about how fast a material gets there.

We start with invented models small enough to check with a calculator, then read real Cu–Ni and Ni–Nb results calculated from published databases. The advanced steps 07–18 then ask how a program can be sure it found the lowest state. You need no software to follow these pages; optional steps for running the calculations yourself are marked. There is no grading and nothing is locked. This page stays available from the Reference button in every step, and the glossary at the end explains the terms used later.

Refresher · First, the vocabulary. The system is the matter you choose to study; everything else is its surroundings. A closed system exchanges energy but no matter. An isolated system exchanges neither. A component is an independent chemical constituent; a phase is a uniform region of the sample (one structure and composition) bounded by interfaces; several coexisting phases can share one phase model (one thermodynamic description). One component can occur in several phases.
Composition tells you the proportions of components inside a phase. Phase amount tells you how much of the sample occupies that phase. Neither automatically equals the area you see in an image.

rows: Internal energy, J; $\Delta U = q + w_{\mathrm{on}}$
Heat q and work are transfers. Work on the system is positive.
$pV$ has units J. $\Delta H = q_p$ only for a closed sample at constant pressure with only pressure–volume work in mechanical equilibrium.
For reversible heat transfer at constant $T$: $\Delta S = q_{\mathrm{rev}}/T$. Irreversible $q/T$ is not a general entropy formula.
F (some texts: A, not the component A)
At fixed $T$, $V$ and component amounts, minimize $F$.
Gibbs energy $G = H - TS = F + pV$, J
At fixed $T$, $p$ and component amounts, minimize $G$.
Amount in mol; $g = G/n$ in J/mol
Here one mole means one mole of atoms; $h = H/n$ and $s = S/n$.
Minimum appropriate potential among allowed states
Not a rate or a prediction of transformation time.

blocks.text: The minimum rules above assume a simple bulk system, with no extra surface, elastic, electrical or magnetic work constraints. For an isolated whole at fixed $U$, $V$ and component amounts, equilibrium instead maximizes $S$. Choose the constraints before the potential.

Why does a closed sample at fixed $T$ and $p$ lower its $G$? Open [[start/lab/second-law|the second-law view of the lab]]: melt part of a sample in a heat bath and watch the total entropy rise exactly when $G$ falls.
Further reading on the thermodynamic potentials:
Further reading on CALPHAD, for when you want the full method:

items: H. L. Lukas, S. G. Fries and B. Sundman (2007): Computational Thermodynamics: The Calphad Method. Cambridge University Press.
N. Saunders and A. P. Miodownik (1998): CALPHAD (Calculation of Phase Diagrams): A Comprehensive Guide. Pergamon.
M. Hillert (2008): Phase Equilibria, Phase Diagrams and Phase Transformations, 2nd edition. Cambridge University Press.
R. Otis and Z.-K. Liu (2017): pycalphad: CALPHAD-based computational thermodynamics in Python. Journal of Open Research Software.

blocks.text: Try this invented state: $U = 1498$ J, $p = 100000$ Pa, $V = 0.00002\ \mathrm{m^3}$, $T = 300$ K, $S = 4$ J/K. Find $pV$, $H$, $TS$, $F$ and $G$. Then check $G - F = pV$. Separately, if $g = -8000$ J/mol, what is $G$ for two moles?

$pV = 2$ J, $H = 1500$ J, $TS = 1200$ J, $F = 298$ J and $G = 300$ J. $G - F = 2$ J. For two moles, $G = -16000$ J. Compare like amounts or molar quantities when selecting a phase. Negative energies are allowed under a consistent reference; $H$ alone misses the entropy contribution.

Two more, on heat, work and entropy. (a) A sample receives 80 J of heat and does 10 J of work on its surroundings. Find $\Delta U$. Must another process with the same $\Delta U$ involve the same heat? (b) A sample receives 900 J of heat reversibly at a constant 300 K. Find $\Delta S$, and give the units of $TS$. Can the sample's entropy ever decrease?

(a) The work on the sample is −10 J, so $\Delta U = 80 - 10 = 70$ J. Another process between the same two states has the same $\Delta U$, but its heat and work can differ as long as their sum is 70 J: heat and work belong to the process, $U$ to the state.

(b) $\Delta S = 900/300 = 3$ J/K. $TS$ has units K × J/K = J, an energy. A sample's entropy can decrease if its surroundings gain at least as much; the second law constrains the isolated whole, not the sample alone.
Glossary · Terms used in later steps. Come back whenever one is unfamiliar.

rows: Share of the sample’s atoms that sit in one phase. The fractions of all phases add up to one.
Fraction of atoms of one element inside a phase, for example x(Ni). Not the same as phase amount.
The composition of the whole sample, counted over all its phases. In a two-phase sample it lies between the two phase compositions.
What “one mole” counts. In this course it is usually one mole of atoms; step 06 also uses moles of formula units. Energies and amounts can only be compared or added on the same basis.
Gibbs energy per mole of atoms, in J/mol. Compare phases only on the same amount basis.

Names of the invented phases in steps 01–04. ALPHA and BETA are ideal solid solutions of A and B (step 03 part B adds a regular-solution term to ALPHA). Step 03 part C reuses SOLID and LIQUID as ideal mixtures of A and B.
Atoms mix randomly with no interaction energy. The only mixing contribution is $RT[(1-x)\ln(1-x) + x\ln x]$, which is negative.

Ideal mixing plus an interaction term $\Omega\,x(1-x)$. A positive Ω makes mixing costly; below a critical temperature, $T_c = \Omega/(2R)$ for this model, one phase can split into two compositions (step 03 part B).
A uniform state that a split could lower is metastable while small changes raise its energy, and unstable where they lower it (inside the spinodal). Steps 03, 07, 09 and 15–17.
How far a state lies below the line of the current answer: the energy gained per mole of atoms by forming it. Steps 07, 12 and 15–17.
How much the total Gibbs energy changes per mole of an element added, for a small addition at fixed T, p and fixed amounts of the other elements.
The tangent to $g(x)$ at a composition meets $x = 0$ at $\mu_{\mathrm A}$ and $x = 1$ at $\mu_{\mathrm B}$.
$\mu_{\mathrm B} - \mu_{\mathrm A}$, the slope of $g(x)$: the Gibbs-energy change when one B atom replaces one A atom on a fixed number of sites.

One straight line touching two curves, or one curve at two points. The touching points are the compositions of two coexisting phases, which then share the same $\mu_{\mathrm A}$ and $\mu_{\mathrm B}$.
The atom balance $f_\alpha x_\alpha + f_\beta x_\beta = z$ solved for the amounts: each phase’s amount is the lever arm on the other side of z divided by the whole tie line.

The advanced steps: a menu is a list of candidate states; its cheapest mixture is a ceiling on the true minimum, and the price line slid below every state is a floor. Steps 10–14; the side cards explain more.
The horizontal line in a temperature–composition diagram that joins the compositions of two coexisting phases at one temperature.
A composition range where one phase model is more stable as two coexisting phases of different composition than as one (step 03 part B; the Cu–Ni dome in step 05).

In a melting range the liquidus is the curve of liquid compositions against temperature (above it, all liquid) and the solidus the curve of solid compositions (below it, all solid); between them liquid and solid coexist. Two ideal phases give a lens shape (step 03 part C).
A temperature and composition where one liquid coexists with two solids. On cooling through it the liquid turns into the two solids at that one temperature.

In a binary at fixed pressure, three phases can coexist only at single temperatures (Gibbs’ phase rule: with two components at fixed pressure, three coexisting phases leave neither temperature nor phase compositions free), so they show up as horizontal lines in a temperature–composition diagram.
Fraction of the boundary sites that hold B atoms.
How many more B atoms the boundary holds than bulk material filling the same number of sites would: positive for enrichment, negative for depletion (step 04).
The sample exchanges atoms with a large supply whose composition and chemical potentials stay fixed.
The total amount of each element is fixed; atoms can only move between regions of the sample.

The energy an open system minimises at fixed T and p: Gibbs energy minus $\mu_i n_i$ for each exchanged element $i$. Textbooks often start from fixed volume instead and write $F - \sum_i \mu_i n_i$; the idea is the same. For a bulk phase in equilibrium with the reservoir it is zero, which is why step 04 works with the excess per boundary site.
In step 04, the grand potential per mole of boundary sites. In the tangent picture it is the vertical gap between the boundary curve and the reservoir tangent.
A set of crystal sites with its own allowed occupants, for example one set for metal atoms and one for vacancies.

A model building block with exactly one kind of occupant on each sublattice. It need not be a stable compound. In a phase with a single sublattice (steps 02–04) the endmembers are simply pure A and pure B.
One copy of the sites a sublattice model describes: 4 for δ (1:1:2) and 13 for μ (2:2:2:6:1) in step 06. Dividing an energy per formula unit by the atoms per formula unit gives J/mol of atoms.

The sublattice model used for phases with several sublattices, such as ordered phases or FCC with its interstitial sites: the Gibbs energy is built from endmember energies plus mixing within each sublattice.

In an ordered phase different sublattices prefer different elements (δ, μ, B2). A line compound has a fixed or almost fixed composition, so its region in a diagram is a thin line (NbNi₈ in step 06, exactly one Nb in nine atoms in its database).
An empty site. Sites that hold only vacancies add no atoms when an energy is converted to J/mol of atoms.

Stable element reference: each element’s enthalpy is measured from its stable form at 298.15 K and 1 bar, so all phases share one reference. It sets the enthalpy of that reference state to zero; its Gibbs energy is −TS there, not zero, because entropy has an absolute zero.
Choosing a model’s parameters to match experiments and other calculations. The result is stored in a TDB database file.
Open-source Python package for CALPHAD calculations: Database reads a TDB file, calculate evaluates phases at given conditions, equilibrium finds the stable combination.
pycalphad results: NP is a phase’s amount fraction, X(NI) the Ni fraction inside that phase, GM the Gibbs energy per mole of atoms.
How densely pycalphad samples trial compositions before refining them. A numerical setting, not a physical quantity.
Database names for face-centred cubic, body-centred cubic and hexagonal close-packed crystal structures.

The ordered form of BCC: cube corners and cube centres form two sublattices, each preferring a different element. In the Ni–Nb database of step 06 it is only a placeholder, with Ni on both sublattices and a constant energy; it was allowed but never appeared.
pycalphad’s word for one coexisting phase in a result; two vertices can share a phase name.
An extra Gibbs-energy term for magnetically ordering phases such as Ni: most negative at low temperature, small near the Curie temperature (where its heat capacity peaks), and not zero above it.
The temperature above which a ferromagnet such as Ni loses its magnetic order.
Many databases give FCC a second set of interstitial sites so that elements like C or N can be added later. In Cu–Ni those sites are all empty.
100000 Pa = 1 bar, used in steps 01–04. 101325 Pa = 1 atm, used for the real alloys. The difference hardly changes these condensed-phase energies.

blocks.text: Some letters have more than one meaning. Marked symbols in later steps (dotted underline) show the meaning that applies there when you hover over or tap them.

rows: {{mu_chem|μ_A}}, {{mu_chem|μ_Ni}}: chemical potential, always with an element subscript (steps 02–04). {{mu_phase|μ phase}} (MU_PHASE): a Ni–Nb phase (step 06).
{{delta_pref|δ}} on its own: the boundary preference energy (step 04). {{delta_phase|δ phase}} (DELTA): a Ni–Nb phase (step 06).
G: Gibbs energy of the whole sample, in J. g and {{gm|GM}}: per mole of atoms. {{g_formula|G_formula}}: per mole of formula units (step 06).
{{g_b|g_b}} and {{x_b|x_b}} belong to the bulk (b = bulk, not boundary). {{g_s|g_s}} belongs to the boundary sites.
x: B fraction inside one phase or region. z: overall B fraction of the whole sample.
Both are phase amount fractions; NP is pycalphad’s name for it.

modules.title: Unary · choose between two phases

blocks.text: In plain words: One pure element can be solid or liquid. At each temperature the one with the lower Gibbs energy wins, and where their two straight lines cross, both are equally good: the melting point. Even there the computer only chooses amounts, never energies. Picture: two straight lines in temperature, crossing once.

Cards you may need: [[card#steeper-line|the steeper line]], [[card#zero-cp|zero heat capacity]], [[card#ends-win|why the ends win]], [[card#amount-vs-mole-fraction|phase amount or mole fraction]], [[card#pure-g|g° = h − Ts and the melting point]].

Problem · Which phase is favoured when we heat one invented component A? Use a closed bulk sample of one mole of A atoms at $p = 100000$ Pa. Only SOLID and LIQUID are allowed, over 800–1200 K. There are no interfaces, pressure dependence or kinetics. The numbers are invented, not taken from a real element.

Approach · At fixed $T$ and $p$, compare $g = h - Ts$ on the same molar reference and [[glossary#amount-basis|amount basis]]. Calculate each branch before choosing the lower one. Which line should fall faster with temperature, and why? Constant within-phase $h$ and $s$ imply zero heat capacity within that phase; this simplification is restricted to the stated domain.

Attempt · Calculate both energies at 900, 1000 and 1100 K. Solve their equality for the crossing temperature. Let $f_{\mathrm L}$ be the liquid phase amount fraction, with $f_{\mathrm S} = 1 - f_{\mathrm L}$. At 900 K, evaluate $g_{\mathrm{mix}} = (1 - f_{\mathrm L})\,g_{\mathrm S} + f_{\mathrm L}\,g_{\mathrm L}$ for $f_{\mathrm L} = 0$, 0.5 and 1. Why must $f_{\mathrm L}$ lie between zero and one?
Use kelvin. $Ts$ has units J/mol atoms, so subtract it from $h$. A negative $g$ can still be the lower energy.
Set $1000 - 10T = 7000 - 16T$ for equality. For mixtures, vary the allowed phase fractions, keeping model parameters and total amount fixed.

The crossing is 1000 K. At 900 K, $g_{\mathrm{mix}} = -8000 + 600\,f_{\mathrm L}$ J/mol atoms: 0, 0.5 and 1 give −8000, −7700 and −7400. The constrained minimum is all solid. A negative fraction is inadmissible even if its computed energy is lower. At equality, every balanced nonnegative split has the same energy, so temperature and pressure do not determine unique phase fractions.

Explore · After your attempt, open the lab below. Drag through the temperatures, compare both branches with the lower one, and check your 900, 1000 and 1100 K values. The [[unary/lab/fractions|phase-fraction chart]] further down draws your $g_{\mathrm{mix}}$ line at the selected temperature. At 1000 K the two energies are equal, so every SOLID/LIQUID split is a minimum; the program simply returns one of them. The Data tab lists the same states solved by two programs, pycalphad and a plain SciPy minimiser.

Interpret and recover · If your phase choice differs, check units, temperature and both branch values before anything else. In pycalphad terms ([[start#why-calphad|the chain sketched in step 00]]), Database reads the models, calculate evaluates any phase, even an unfavoured one, and equilibrium searches the allowed phases for the minimum that respects the amounts. Excluding LIQUID at 1100 K asks a different, restricted question; it does not give the unrestricted minimum.

A calculation restricted to SOLID alone, for example at 1100 K where the liquid is lower, describes a declared, restricted model, a superheated solid: its minimum can only be higher than the full one. See the card [[card#restricted|why a restricted calculation can only be higher]].

More practice. Calculate both energies at 1050 K and at 975 K and say which phase is lower. Then find the mistake in each of two reports. Report 1: “At 900 K the solid has $g = -8$ J/mol.” Report 2: “At 1000 K the equilibrium is $f_{\mathrm S} = 0.8$ and $f_{\mathrm L} = 0.4$.”
At 1050 K, $g_{\mathrm S} = -9500$ and $g_{\mathrm L} = -9800$ J/mol atoms, so liquid is lower. At 975 K they are −8750 and −8600 J/mol atoms, so solid is lower.

Report 1 mixes units: the solid has −8000 J/mol, which is −8 kJ/mol, not −8 J/mol. Report 2 breaks the balance: $f_{\mathrm S}$ and $f_{\mathrm L}$ must add up to one. At 1000 K any split with $f_{\mathrm S} + f_{\mathrm L} = 1$ is an equally good minimum, but 0.8 and 0.4 add up to 1.2. A low energy is only meaningful for a state that respects the amounts and the bounds.
Next · Composition brings another constraint. Invented lines like these cannot predict a real alloy; that needs assessed inputs, which arrive in steps 05 and 06.
Advanced step [[menu|10]] reads this same problem with many candidate states instead of two.

modules.title: Binary · composition and chemical potential

blocks.text: In plain words: Mixing two elements adds a bonus from counting arrangements, so a mixture can be lower than its unmixed parts. The tangent to the curve at your composition tells you what one more atom of A or of B is worth. Picture: a sagging curve and a straight line touching it at your composition.

Cards you may need: [[card#endmember|endmember and reference energy]], [[card#zero-log|0 ln 0 = 0]], [[card#mixing-negative|negative mixing G]], [[card#x-ln-x|where x ln x comes from]], [[card#chemical-potential|chemical potential]].

Problem · How does adding a second invented component change the energy question? We allow only one phase, an ideal solid solution called ALPHA, at $T = 1000$ K and $p = 100000$ Pa, per mole of A and B atoms. The model is invented, and because only ALPHA is allowed this is not a full equilibrium calculation.

Define $x = n_{\mathrm B}/(n_{\mathrm A} + n_{\mathrm B})$, the B atom mole fraction within ALPHA; A has fraction $1 - x$. A [[glossary#phase-amount-fraction-f|phase amount fraction]] describes how much sample is in a phase, like $f_{\mathrm L}$ in [[unary#attempt|step 01]]. For two balanced trial regions, $z = f_1 x_1 + f_2 x_2$ with $f_1 + f_2 = 1$. Balance alone does not establish coexistence, and $x$ is not an image-area fraction (see the [[start#refresher|step 00 refresher]]). Here $z$ is the [[glossary#overall-composition-z|overall composition]] of the whole sample.

rows: 1000, 13000 J/mol atoms; 10, 10 J/(mol atoms K), so $g_{\mathrm A} = h_{\mathrm A} - T s_{\mathrm A} = -9000$ and $g_{\mathrm B} = +3000$ at 1000 K

blocks.text: At the pure ends use the limit $0 \ln 0 = 0$ for the energy; never evaluate $\ln 0$. There the slope of the curve is infinite and the chemical potential of the missing element tends to $-\infty$, while that of the element present stays finite (its pure value: $\mu_{\mathrm A}=-9000$ J/mol at $x=0$). Formulas with $\ln x$ cannot be evaluated there, so the lab covers $x = 0.01$ to 0.99 in steps of 0.01.

A chemical potential {{mu_chem|μ_i}} is the change of total $G$ on adding component $i$ at fixed $T$, $p$ and the other component amount. At fixed total occupied sites, replacing A by B uses $\mu_{\mathrm B} - \mu_{\mathrm A}$. For a differentiable molar curve {{g_b|g_b}}: $g_{\mathrm b}' = \mu_{\mathrm B} - \mu_{\mathrm A}$, $\mu_{\mathrm A} = g_{\mathrm b} - x\,g_{\mathrm b}'$ and $\mu_{\mathrm B} = g_{\mathrm b} + (1-x)\,g_{\mathrm b}'$. Here $\mu_{\mathrm A} = -9000 + 8314.5\ln(1-x)$ and $\mu_{\mathrm B} = 3000 + 8314.5\ln x$.

Tangent and chemical potentials · Why are the tangent’s ends the chemical potentials? The tangent at $x_0$ is the line $y = g_{\mathrm b}(x_0) + g_{\mathrm b}'(x_0)\,(x - x_0)$. At $x = 0$ it gives $g_{\mathrm b} - x_0\,g_{\mathrm b}' = \mu_{\mathrm A}$; at $x = 1$ it gives $g_{\mathrm b} + (1 - x_0)\,g_{\mathrm b}' = \mu_{\mathrm B}$. So both chemical potentials can be read where the tangent meets the two edges of the diagram. The same picture returns in step 03 for [[twophase#approach|two phases]] and in step 04 for [[boundary#where-the-odds-formula-comes-from|a grain boundary]].

The tangent at the worked point $x=0.10$: its end heights are $\mu_A\approx-9876.0$ and $\mu_B\approx-16144.8$ J/mol, and the dashed line is the straight line between the pure ends. Where does the mixing bonus that pulls the curve below that line come from? Open [[binary/lab/counter|the arrangement counter]].

image.alt: The bulk curve of ALPHA at 1000 K, its tangent at x = 0.10 meeting x = 0 at μA ≈ −9876.0 and x = 1 at μB ≈ −16144.8 J/mol, and the dashed straight line between the pure ends

blocks.text: Approach · Separate the reference term from the mixing term. Keep atom basis and natural logarithms consistent. Ideal enthalpy of mixing is zero, but ideal mixing Gibbs energy is negative inside the domain; total enthalpy and total energy need not vanish.

Attempt · At $x = 0.20$, use $q = -0.50040242$ to calculate the reference, mixing and total molar energies. Use $\ln(0.20/0.80) = -1.38629436$ in $g_{\mathrm b}' = 12000 + 8314.5\ln[x/(1-x)]$ to find the [[glossary#exchange-slope|exchange slope]] and its sign. For 2 mol of atoms at $z = 0.20$, find the A/B amounts. The slope changes sign somewhere between the two pure ends: does that mean two phases form?
First multiply each [[glossary#endmember|endmember]] energy (here pure A and pure B) by its atom fraction; then add $RTq$. For amounts, multiply total moles by the composition.

Both $\mu$ values matter because a B atom entering a filled site displaces an A atom. A derivative is a local exchange comparison; it has not compared all possible phase combinations. [[twophase#approach|Step 03]] makes that comparison.

The reference is −6600 J/mol atoms, mixing is approximately −4160.596 J/mol atoms and $g_{\mathrm b} \approx$ −10760.596 J/mol atoms. The exchange slope is approximately +473.656 J/mol atoms. The two-mole sample contains 0.40 mol B and 1.60 mol A. Only ALPHA was allowed, so no two-phase coexistence follows from a derivative sign change.

Where the slope changes sign: between $x = 0.19$ (about −56 J/mol atoms) and $x = 0.20$ (about +474). That is the minimum of this one curve. It is not the composition the sample takes: a closed sample’s composition is fixed by its amounts of A and B, and with only ALPHA allowed it stays homogeneous at that composition.

Explore · After your attempt, open the lab. At $x = 0.50$ check the slope against 12000 J/mol atoms; at $x = 0.20$ compare your rounded answer. The chart shows the total curve; the Reference line and Mixing term buttons add the two parts. The [[binary/lab/slope|exchange-slope chart]] further down shows where the slope changes sign. The tangent at your composition meets the left edge ($x = 0$) at $\mu_{\mathrm A}$ and the right edge ($x = 1$) at $\mu_{\mathrm B}$.

Interpret and recover · If you used only the weighted endmember energies, add the missing mixing term. Convert kJ/mol to J/mol before judging differences. For example, at $x = 0.10$ the curve gives $g_{\mathrm b} = -10502.902$ J/mol; a report of −10.50 kJ/mol differs by about 2.902 J/mol, which is just rounding to 0.01 kJ/mol. For a balanced trial at $z = 0.20$, $x_1 = 0.10$ and $x_2 = 0.50$ give $f_1 = 0.75$ and $f_2 = 0.25$; that checks amounts without proving equilibrium.
Next · With one phase, the composition is fixed by the amounts. [[twophase|Step 03]] allows a second phase and asks when the sample splits in two.
Advanced step [[price-line|11]] shows the tangent's two end heights coming out of an optimisation.

modules.title: Two phases · common tangent and lever rule

blocks.text: In plain words: Sometimes a sample does better by splitting into two regions of different composition. The best split is found by one straight line that touches the curves twice, and the lever rule says how much of each region forms. Picture: two curves and one line resting on both.

Cards you may need: [[card#lever-rule|the lever rule]], [[card#common-tangent|the common tangent]], [[card#chord-rule|the chord rule]], [[card#metastable-unstable|metastable or unstable]], [[card#newtons-method|Newton's method]].

Problem · Why does a sample sometimes split into two phases, and how much of each forms? Step 02 allowed only one phase. Now allow two invented phases, ALPHA and BETA, at 1000 K and 100000 Pa, per mole of atoms. The sample has a fixed overall B fraction {{z_overall|z}}.
Heads-up: this step has four parts. You can stop after any of them and come back; the lab has a tab for each part.

items: Part A · two different phases: from the problem below to its worked answer (main, about 30 min).
[[twophase#part-b-one-phase-model-two-phases|Part B]] · one phase model, two coexisting phases (main, about 20 min).
[[twophase#part-c-melting-and-the-lens|Part C]] · melting, the lens, and reading a phase diagram (main, about 20 min).

[[twophase#part-d-from-scratch-and-with-pycalphad|Part D]] · how a program finds the split: one lens point from scratch and with pycalphad (optional, about 20 min; step 10 starts from its grid, but repeats what it needs).

blocks.text: A split into two regions is allowed only if it keeps the amounts: $f_\alpha + f_\beta = 1$ and $f_\alpha x_\alpha + f_\beta x_\beta = z$, with both fractions between 0 and 1. Solving these two balances for $f_\beta = (z - x_\alpha)/(x_\beta - x_\alpha)$ is the [[glossary#lever-rule|lever rule]]; it is just the balance, not yet an equilibrium. The figure after the worked answer draws it as two lever arms. The split’s energy per mole of atoms is $f_\alpha\,g_\alpha(x_\alpha) + f_\beta\,g_\beta(x_\beta)$.

Approach · Compare the homogeneous states with splits at the same $z$. A split’s energy lies on the straight line joining its two points $(x_\alpha, g_\alpha)$ and $(x_\beta, g_\beta)$, at the overall composition $z$. The lowest such line touches both curves: a common tangent. Touching means it is one line for both phases, so it meets $x = 0$ and $x = 1$ at the same values, $\mu_{\mathrm A}$ and $\mu_{\mathrm B}$ (as in [[binary#tangent-and-chemical-potentials|step 02]]); therefore {{mu_chem|μ_A}} and {{mu_chem|μ_B}} are the same in both phases and atoms gain nothing by moving between them. That is the condition for two phases to coexist.
Attempt · Work at $z = 0.5$:

items: Homogeneous ALPHA at $x = 0.5$: find $g_\alpha$ using $q(0.5) = -0.69314718$.

A split with $x_\alpha = 0.2$ and $x_\beta = 0.8$: find $f_\alpha$ and $f_\beta$ from the balance, then the split energy. Use $g_\alpha(0.2) = g_\beta(0.8) =$ −10760.596 J/mol atoms. Which state is lower, and by how much?
With the same endpoints, find $f_\alpha$ and $f_\beta$ at $z = 0.35$. Is $z = 0.1$ possible with these endpoints?

The best split uses $x_\alpha \approx$ 0.19104 and $x_\beta \approx$ 0.80896, with energy −10762.730 J/mol atoms. Why is it lower than your 0.2/0.8 split, and what are $\mu_{\mathrm A}$ and $\mu_{\mathrm B}$ there?

blocks.text: Balance first: $f_\beta = (z - x_\alpha)/(x_\beta - x_\alpha)$ and $f_\alpha = 1 - f_\beta$. Then multiply each region’s energy by its fraction and add.
On a common tangent both touching points have the same slope. Here $g_\alpha$ and $g_\beta$ are mirror images, so the tangent is horizontal and meets $x = 0$ and $x = 1$ at the same energy.

Homogeneous ALPHA at 0.5: $-9000 + 6000 + 8314.5 \times (-0.69314718) =$ −8763.172 J/mol atoms. The 0.2/0.8 split has $f_\alpha = f_\beta = 0.5$ and energy −10760.596 J/mol atoms, about 1997 J/mol lower, so splitting wins. At $z = 0.35$, $f_\beta = (0.35 - 0.2)/0.6 = 0.25$ and $f_\alpha = 0.75$. At $z = 0.1$ the balance gives $f_\beta = -1/6$, which is impossible: these endpoints cannot make that sample.

Moving the endpoints to the touching points 0.19104/0.80896 lowers the line to −10762.730 J/mol atoms, about 2.13 J/mol below the 0.2/0.8 split. Because the tangent is horizontal, $\mu_{\mathrm A} = \mu_{\mathrm B} =$ −10762.730 J/mol in both phases. Every $z$ between 0.19104 and 0.80896 splits into these same two compositions; only the amounts change, by the lever rule.

Part B: one phase model, two phases · The same idea works with only one phase model. In a [[glossary#regular-solution|regular-solution model]] ALPHA gets an extra mixing term $\Omega\,x(1-x)$, with $\Omega = 20000$ J/mol, that penalises mixing. (CALPHAD papers and databases write this term as the first Redlich–Kister parameter, $L_0\,x(1-x)$, and add $L_1\,x(1-x)(x_{\mathrm A}-x_{\mathrm B})$ and higher terms when the data need them.) Below about 1203 K the mixing part of $g(x)$ ($g$ minus its straight reference line, [[binary/lab/tangent|as in the step 02 lab]]) develops a hump; a common tangent then touches the curve twice, and the sample separates into two ALPHA regions with different compositions: two coexisting phases described by one phase model. This is called a {{misc_gap|miscibility gap}}. Above that temperature the hump disappears and one homogeneous phase is stable. (The full $g(x)$ only bends a little, because the straight $12000\,x$ reference term dominates; the lab therefore shows the mixing part, which has the same touching points; its Full g(x) switch shows the whole curve.)
The bending of the curve decides stability. Open [[twophase/lab/stability|the stability view]] and raise $\Omega/RT$: above 2 the binodal and the spinodal appear, with metastable bands between them.
Predict before you open [[twophase/lab/part-b|part B of the lab]]: as the temperature rises towards 1203 K, do the two compositions move closer together or further apart?
They move together. At 600 K they are 0.021 and 0.979; they meet at $x = 0.5$ at $T_{\mathrm c} = \Omega/(2R) \approx 1203$ K. Above $T_{\mathrm c}$ one homogeneous phase is stable.

Part C: melting and the lens · Part A compared two invented phases at one temperature. Now let a solid and a liquid both change with temperature, each an ideal solution of A and B. Component A is the one from [[unary#problem|step 01]]: it melts at 1000 K. Its two lines were stated for 800–1200 K there; parts C and D use them up to 1800 K as a declared extension of the invented model. Component B is invented: solid $h = 2000$, $s = 10$; liquid $h = 20000$, $s = 20$ (J/mol atoms and J/(mol atoms K)), so it melts at 1800 K. Below 1000 K the solid curve lies lower at every composition; above 1800 K the liquid does. In between the two curves cross, and the common tangent touches the liquid on the A-rich side and the solid on the B-rich side: the solid is richer in the component with the higher melting point. Collecting the two touching points at every temperature draws a lens. Its upper edge is the liquidus (above it, all liquid) and its lower edge the solidus (below it, all solid). [[twophase/lab/part-c|Part C of the lab]] draws it as you change the temperature.

Reading a phase diagram · Plot the two touching compositions at every temperature against $T$ and you have a phase diagram. Outside the curve one phase is stable; inside it the sample splits. At a given $T$ and $z$ inside, the horizontal line between the two boundary compositions is a [[glossary#tie-line|tie line]]: its ends give the compositions of the two regions, and the [[glossary#lever-rule|lever rule]] gives their amounts.

Real diagrams combine several such regions. In the [[cuni#reading-the-diagram|Cu–Ni diagram of step 05]] you will see both kinds: a low-temperature miscibility gap with two FCC compositions, like part B, and at high temperature a {{lens|liquid/FCC lens}} like part C. Where three phases meet, for example one liquid and two solids at a [[glossary#eutectic|eutectic]], they can coexist only at one temperature; [[ninb#reading-the-diagram|step 06]] shows two.

Part D: from scratch and with pycalphad · How does a program actually find the two touching points? Take part C at 1400 K and a sample with overall composition $z = 0.40$. The same answer can be reached in four ways, and [[twophase/lab/part-d|part D of the lab]] plays each one next to pycalphad’s answer:

items: Try every split: pair each trial solid composition with every liquid composition, keep the pairs the lever rule allows and take the one with the lowest energy. Simple, but slow, and only as fine as the trial compositions.

Grid and linear programme: put candidate compositions of both phases on a grid and find the cheapest mixture of them that keeps all atoms and all B atoms. Energy and both balances are linear in the amounts, so this is a linear programme, which needs no first guess and is not told which phases appear. Never met a linear programme? The optional [[lp-primer|LP primer]] starts from scratch.

Equal chemical potentials: solve $\mu_{\mathrm A}^{S} = \mu_{\mathrm A}^{L}$ and $\mu_{\mathrm B}^{S} = \mu_{\mathrm B}^{L}$ for the two compositions with Newton’s method. Each step replaces the two equations by straight lines and solves those; from the rough first guess in the lab it reaches the touching points in a handful of steps. (In the notebook, SciPy’s fsolve takes such steps for you.)
Step by step through temperature: start from the 1400 K answer and use each answer as the first guess at the next temperature. The touching points at all temperatures draw the lens.

blocks.text: pycalphad does the same for any database: it evaluates every phase on a grid of trial compositions (for a simple binary phase 122 with the default settings: 60 sampled, 60 along the composition axis and the two pure ends; step 13 has the numbers), finds the best combination as in the second method, and refines it by solving the equal-chemical-potential equations as in the third. For this model the two routes agree in every digit the lab shows.
The grid's linear programme returns more than amounts: two prices that draw a straight line under the grid's dots. Advanced step [[menu|10]] starts from exactly this grid.
Predict before you play the grid method: if the candidate compositions are only 0.2 apart, what does the linear programme report for $z = 0.40$ at 1400 K?

The true split is lower by only about 39 J/mol atoms. From a spacing of 0.05 on, the grid finds the split, and its energy approaches the exact value from above.

Part B: move the temperature and watch the two compositions draw the miscibility gap in the phase diagram. Part C: do the same for melting and watch the lens appear between 1000 and 1800 K. modules.title: Grain boundary · open exchange or closed inventory

blocks.text: In plain words: A grain boundary has its own sites, which can hold more or less B than the bulk around it. Whether the boundary trades atoms with a huge reservoir or shares a small closed cell changes which energy you minimise. Picture: a thin layer of sites between two blocks of crystal.

Cards you may need: [[card#site-occupancy-excess|site, occupancy or excess]], [[card#grand-potential|the grand potential]], [[card#odds-theta|θ from the odds]], [[card#boundary-b-source|where the boundary's B comes from]], [[card#same-inventory|the same inventory]].

Problem · Will an invented boundary enrich in B, and where do those atoms come from? Keep the invented ALPHA bulk from [[binary#problem|step 02]] at 1000 K and 100000 Pa. The cell is periodic, like one repeating unit of a polycrystal, so it contains two equivalent boundaries. Each boundary has 100 sites and 20 nm² of area. The bulk has 8000 sites; the whole cell has 8200 sites and 40 nm² of boundary. The boundary is invented, not a real grain boundary of any element.
Heads-up: here {{delta_pref|δ}} is the boundary preference, an energy. In step 06 the same letter names a Ni–Nb phase (the δ phase). Marked symbols show their meaning on hover or tap.

Occupancy $\theta$ is the B fraction of boundary sites; {{x_b|x_b}} is the B fraction of bulk sites. Every site holds A or B, so adding B replaces A, as in the [[glossary#exchange-slope|exchange slope]] of step 02. Counts are averages and need not be whole numbers. Convert counts to moles with $N_{\mathrm{Av}} = 6.02214076\times10^{23}\ \mathrm{mol^{-1}}$ before multiplying by a J/mol energy.

Two experiments. In the open one, the cell sits against a large reservoir with fixed $x_{\mathrm b}$, {{mu_chem|μ_A}} and {{mu_chem|μ_B}}: atoms can enter or leave, and the open cell minimises its [[glossary#grand-potential|grand potential]] (the “open to a reservoir” sketch in the [[start#refresher|step 00 refresher]]). In the closed one no atoms enter or leave: the A and B totals are fixed, B that moves to the boundaries must come from the bulk, and the cell minimises its total $G$. Because the two minimise different energies on different bases, never rank one against the other.

rows: $g_{\mathrm b}(\theta) + \delta\,\theta + \eta$, with the preference {{delta_pref|δ}} $= -5000$ J/mol boundary sites and the baseline {{eta|η}} $= 0$ in this step
$200(\theta - x_{\mathrm b})$ across both boundaries; $5(\theta - x_{\mathrm b})$ atom/nm²
$g_{\mathrm s}(\theta) - (1-\theta)\,\mu_{\mathrm A} - \theta\,\mu_{\mathrm B}$, J/mol boundary sites: the grand potential per boundary site

blocks.text: The excess compares the boundary with bulk material filling the same number of sites. A negative excess means depletion relative to that reference, not a negative B count. Other excess conventions exist; this one is chosen for simple counting. Per boundary the excess is $100(\theta - x_{\mathrm b})$ B atoms on 20 nm², that is $5(\theta - x_{\mathrm b})$ atoms per nm²; dividing by $N_{\mathrm{Av}}$ and converting nm² to m² gives mol/m².

Approach · Predict enrichment from the negative preference, then count atoms before energy. In open equilibrium the odds of B on a boundary site obey $\frac{\theta}{1-\theta} = \frac{x_{\mathrm b}}{1-x_{\mathrm b}}\exp(5000/8314.5)$, with factor 1.82459687 supplied. For a closed cell initially at $x_0 = 0.10$ and $\theta_0 = 0.25$, $B_{\mathrm{tot}} = 8000\,x_0 + 200\,\theta_0$ and $x_{\mathrm b}(\theta) = (B_{\mathrm{tot}} - 200\,\theta)/8000$.

Where the odds formula comes from · At the open minimum, moving one more B onto a boundary site (and one A off it) must gain nothing against the reservoir, so $d\varphi/d\theta = 0$, which means $g_{\mathrm s}'(\theta) = \mu_{\mathrm B} - \mu_{\mathrm A}$. With $g_{\mathrm s}'(\theta) = g_{\mathrm b}'(\theta) + \delta$, where {{delta_pref|δ}} is the boundary preference, the reservoir value $\mu_{\mathrm B} - \mu_{\mathrm A} = g_{\mathrm b}'(x_{\mathrm b})$, and $g_{\mathrm b}'(x) = 12000 + RT\ln[x/(1-x)]$ from [[binary#attempt|step 02]], the 12000 cancels: $RT\ln\frac{\theta}{1-\theta} + \delta = RT\ln\frac{x_{\mathrm b}}{1-x_{\mathrm b}}$. Taking exponentials gives the odds formula, known in the literature as the McLean (or Langmuir–McLean) segregation isotherm, with $\delta$ in the role of the segregation energy, and factor $\exp(-\delta/RT) = \exp(5000/8314.5)$. In a picture: the boundary settles where a line parallel to the reservoir tangent touches $g_{\mathrm s}$, and φ is the vertical gap between the two lines (the figure below).

The closed cell obeys the same condition (differentiating $G_{\mathrm{cell}}$ with $x_{\mathrm b} = (B_{\mathrm{tot}} - 200\,\theta)/8000$ gives $dG_{\mathrm{cell}}/d\theta \propto g_{\mathrm s}'(\theta) - g_{\mathrm b}'(x_{\mathrm b})$), but its bulk fraction depends on $\theta$. You can solve it by hand by iteration (after your attempt, the lab’s Closed cell by hand view steps through it): start with $x_{\mathrm b} = x_0$, compute $\theta$ from the odds formula, update $x_{\mathrm b}$, and repeat. Four or five rounds settle to $\theta \approx 0.17161$.
Attempt · Work through both cells:

items: Open cell at $x_{\mathrm b} = 0.10$: find the odds, $\theta$ and the excess per nm². Would {{delta_pref|δ}} $= 0$ give enrichment?
Closed cell from the setup above: find the initial A and B totals.
Closed cell at a trial $\theta = 0.35$: find the bulk $x_{\mathrm b}$ and both B counts. What goes wrong if you keep $x_{\mathrm b} = 0.10$?
A different boundary state could have a baseline {{eta|η}} $= 2000$ J/mol boundary sites (the extension below compares one). How much would that add per mole of all 8200 cell sites?

blocks.text: For odds $r$, $\theta = r/(1+r)$. For the closed trial, subtract boundary B from the fixed total before dividing by bulk sites.
Both boundaries contribute 200 sites and 40 nm². For the baseline, 200 of 8200 sites carry the extra 2000 J/mol; do not assign it to every site.

Open odds $\approx 0.20273299$, $\theta \approx 0.16856026$ and excess $\approx 0.3428013$ atom/nm² ($5.69235\times10^{-7}$ mol/m²). At zero preference $\theta = x_{\mathrm b}$ and the excess is zero. Closed initial B=850 and A=7350. Trial $\theta = 0.35$ gives boundary B = 70, bulk B = 780 and $x_{\mathrm b} = 0.0975$; fixing $x_{\mathrm b} = 0.10$ would incorrectly give 870 B. A totals still equal 7350. The baseline contributes $200 \times 2000/8200 =$ 48.78049 J/mol all cell sites.

The closed cell at $x_0 = 0.10$ settles at $\theta \approx 0.17161$ and $x_{\mathrm b} \approx 0.10196$: boundary B≈34.3215 plus bulk B≈815.6785 equals 850 within rounding. Two numerical methods give it: minimising $G$ directly gives $\theta =$ 0.17160753314081367, and solving the exchange condition above gives 0.17160752408695693. They agree to about $10^{-8}$; the lab shows both as a check.

Explore · Open the lab and move the starting composition. Both cells start with boundary occupancy $\theta_0 = 0.25$. Where the selected $\theta$ is below 0.25 the boundaries give up B: the open cell returns it to the reservoir, the closed cell passes it to the bulk. Where $\theta$ is above 0.25 they take B instead. The two occupancy curves nearly coincide because the bulk is large; compare the atom ledgers to see the difference. Excess values are per boundary, while the ledgers count both boundaries. The Tangent picture view shows the open cell with the tangent of [[binary#tangent-and-chemical-potentials|step 02]]: move the boundary preference and watch where the boundary settles. The Closed cell by hand view steps through the hand method round by round.

blocks.label: Extension · compare two candidate boundary states

blocks.text: Try subtracting the supplied energies for two synthetic uniform boundary states: I has {{eta|η}} $= 0$, {{delta_pref|δ}} $= -5000$; II has {{eta|η}} $= 2000$, {{delta_pref|δ}} $= -10000$ J/mol boundary sites. Both share geometry, references and initial $\theta_0 = 0.25$. At 850 B, $\bar g_{\mathrm I} = -10541.72679$ and $\bar g_{\mathrm{II}} = -10519.50695$ J/mol all sites; at 2050 B (a cell started at $x_0 = 0.25$, $\theta_0 = 0.25$), they are −10713.32958 and −10718.80845. Compare within each inventory row. II−I is +22.21984 in the first row and −5.47887 in the second, selecting I then II among these two candidates. Each state must adjust its own final $x_{\mathrm b}$. A crossing between two uniform alternatives is not a study of a real boundary transition. The lab shows state I only.

blocks.label: Practice · a second open and closed cell

blocks.text: Try open $x_{\mathrm b} = 0.20$ with the same factor: $\theta \approx 0.31325719$ and excess $\approx 0.566286$ atom/nm². Separately start a closed cell at $x_0 = 0.20$, $\theta_0 = 0.20$: $B_{\mathrm{tot}} = 1640$. Trial $\theta = 0.40$ gives boundary B = 80, bulk B = 1560, $x_{\mathrm b} = 0.195$. Keeping bulk at 0.20 would violate the inventory. If counts disagree, check the two-boundary factor before adjusting any energy.

From model to material · Everything in steps 01–04 used invented numbers, so the calculations show how the reasoning works, not what a real alloy does. A real question, say about Cu at a nickel grain boundary, needs four things before any claim, and our invented models supply none of them.

rows: The exact alloy, the quantity to explain (for example, how much Cu sits at one kind of boundary), the boundary geometry, and data we may use
An assessed Gibbs-energy model for the alloy over the right temperatures and compositions, giving the chemical potentials of the reservoir ([[cuni|step 05]] reads one for Cu–Ni)
Site counts and area, boundary energies or excesses for each boundary structure, on the same reference as the bulk, with independent evidence
A planned calculation with conservation checks, compared with data that were not used to build the model

blocks.text: Sort each statement into invented-model result, missing evidence, or unsupported real claim: (a) in the invented cell with 850 B atoms, state I has the lower energy; (b) an assessed Ni–Cu bulk model valid at the temperature and composition of interest; (c) Ni–Cu grain boundaries change structure at $x_0 = 0.216$; (d) two real boundary-state free energies, measured from one common reference; (e) the Cu concentration at an actual nickel grain boundary. Then: why does an energy crossing between two boundary states not yet show a real transition?

(a) Invented-model result. (b) Missing evidence: the bulk model. (c) Unsupported real claim: the crossing belongs to the invented states. (d) Missing evidence: the boundary model, with both states on one reference. (e) A question these models cannot answer; it needs all four rows of the table.

An energy crossing compares two uniform states. At a fixed inventory, a boundary that is partly in one state and partly in the other can have a lower energy than either uniform state near the crossing, so a real change may happen over a range of compositions rather than at one point. Showing a transition needs that coexistence analysis, real state energies and independent evidence.

Wrap-up · Explain which energy each experiment minimises (the [[start#refresher|step 00 refresher]] sketches all four cases; in the lab each cell’s energy sits in a closed “energy value” reveal), how zero preference changes the excess, and why the open and closed energies cannot be ranked. Then write one sentence these invented calculations support and one claim about a real material they cannot support. (A real boundary transition would need real boundary energies and evidence of coexistence; an invented energy crossing provides neither.) Next we read real bulk-material results; the invented boundary parameters are not carried over.

modules.title: Cu–Ni · reading a published-database calculation

blocks.text: In plain words: Now the energies come from a published database for copper and nickel, not from an invented model. You read a real phase diagram, check the atom balance of a saved calculation, and see what one modelling choice, magnetism, changes. Picture: the Cu–Ni diagram with its lens and its low-temperature gap.

Cards you may need: [[card#tdb-line|reading a TDB line]], [[card#calphad-database|CALPHAD and databases]], [[card#sigma|what Σ means]], [[card#f-np|f and NP]], [[card#phase-model-state|phase, phase model, grid state]].

Problem · How do assessed material inputs change the questions we asked with invented parameters? This step reads a Cu–Ni calculation made in advance with pycalphad from a published database (Mey’s [[glossary#assessment-tdb|assessment]], as adapted by Hallstedt). Nothing is calculated live in this step. Try the balance exercise before opening the answer or the energy plots.

What changes with a real alloy: instead of invented phases with numbers you can check by hand, each phase now has a model assessed from experiments, several candidate phases compete at once, and a program finds the combination with the lowest $G$ ([[start#why-calphad|the chain in step 00]]). You read its saved output: which phases appear, their compositions $x(\mathrm{Ni})$ and their amounts [[glossary#np-x-gm|NP]]. Terms such as {{fcc|FCC_A1}}, {{vertex|vertex}} and {{magnetic|magnetic contribution}} are marked; hover or tap them.

The calculation used 101325 Pa and one mole of atoms, 81 temperatures from 300 to 1900 K (20 K steps) and 61 overall $x(\mathrm{Ni})$ values from 0.005 to 0.995, with pycalphad’s sampling setting [[glossary#pdens|pdens]]=60. LIQUID, FCC_A1, BCC_A2 and HCP_A3 were allowed, with and without the magnetic contribution. The pressure is a lesson choice; the published figure does not state one.

In pycalphad output, GM is the Gibbs energy per mole of atoms, NP is a phase’s amount fraction on the same basis, and X(NI) is the Ni fraction inside that phase. The FCC model has a second set of interstitial sites (a second [[glossary#sublattice|sublattice]]) that holds only [[glossary#vacancy-va|vacancies]] here; databases include it so that elements such as C or N can be added later. Empty sites add no atoms, so its energy is per one mole of atoms, not two; [[ninb#approach|step 06]] does the same bookkeeping for ordered phases. Energies use the [[glossary#ser|stable element reference (SER)]], which fixes each element’s enthalpy zero; it does not make the Gibbs energy zero at 298.15 K.

Approach · First fix bulk composition and temperature. Multiple phase compositions can share that bulk composition if their amounts balance both elements. Use $\sum_i f_i x_i = z$ and $\sum_i f_i = 1$, the balance of [[twophase#problem|step 03]]. Comparing the lowest point anywhere along an energy curve would change the alloy composition and answer a different question (see [[binary#attempt|step 02’s worked answer]]).

headers: Supplied magnetic-on sample at 600 K, bulk x(Ni)=0.5

blocks.text: Reading the diagram · Here is the saved calculation for both magnetic settings. Each dot is the composition of a phase found at one grid temperature: blue for liquid, orange for FCC. Where the sample is a single phase, its dots fill the area. In a two-phase region no single phase has that composition, so the area stays empty; at a given temperature, the dots on its two sides are the two coexisting compositions (in the literature, two composition sets of one phase where it is FCC on both sides), the ends of a tie line ([[twophase#reading-a-phase-diagram|step 03]]). The edges are only as sharp as the 20 K and composition grid.

image.alt: Cu–Ni sampled phase compositions versus temperature and Ni atom mole fraction, comparing magnetic-on and magnetic-off calculations.

blocks.text: Read it from the top. At high temperature everything is liquid. The empty band between the blue and orange dots is the {{lens|liquid/FCC lens}}: liquid and FCC coexist there with different compositions, and the common tangent joins two different curves, as in [[twophase#part-c-melting-and-the-lens|step 03 part C]]. Below it one FCC phase spans all compositions, which is possible because Cu and Ni share the same crystal structure. The empty dome at the bottom is the {{misc_gap|miscibility gap}}: FCC separates into a Cu-rich and a Ni-rich composition, as in [[twophase#part-b-one-phase-model-two-phases|step 03 part B]]. Compare the top of the dome with and without magnetism; the attempt below asks what that difference means. After your attempt, the results explorer opens with the same calculation as a [[cuni/lab/map|clickable map]]: pick any temperature and composition to see the phases, their amounts and the tie line, or press play to cool or heat at that composition.

Attempt · Reconstruct the Ni and Cu fractions from the 600 K table above. Why can both rows be called FCC_A1? Would switching off the {{magnetic|magnetic contribution}} necessarily remove the two-FCC region (the {{misc_gap|miscibility gap}})? How does reading this assessed calculation differ from the [[boundary#wrap-up|invented boundary model]], and from testing against experiment?
Multiply each phase composition by its atom-mole amount fraction before summing. For Cu use $1 - x(\mathrm{Ni})$.

Two compositions of the same phase model can be selected, as in [[twophase#part-b-one-phase-model-two-phases|step 03 part B]]; a different composition need not mean a different crystal structure. Chemical and magnetic energy contributions both enter the original model.

The weighted Ni sum is 0.5 and Cu sum is 0.5 to within $10^{-6}$; the fractions sum to one. Both vertices are FCC_A1 at different compositions. Magnetic-off also has two FCC compositions at 600 K (about 0.406223 and 0.764343 with fractions 0.738142 and 0.261858), so the chemical model already demixes. Magnetism changes these calculated results.

At 1540 K and overall $x(\mathrm{Ni}) = 0.5$, the lowest sampled temperature at which liquid and FCC coexist (at 1520 K there is no liquid yet) has approximately 0.0978183 liquid at $x(\mathrm{Ni}) = 0.368010$ and 0.902182 FCC at 0.514311. Use the full precision in the saved results (the reveal below, or the 1540 K button under [[cuni/lab/samples|Saved samples]] in the results explorer) for the same balance check. The saved 1500 K state is all FCC; 1600 K is all liquid.

Reading this calculation tells you what the assessed model predicts at these conditions. The step 04 boundary model was invented, so it predicts nothing about a real material. Neither is a test against experiment: that needs measured compositions or temperatures compared with these numbers, and the model parameters were themselves chosen to fit some of those measurements.

Read Gibbs energies on a shared J/mol atom basis. The pure-Ni panel marks the source {{curie|Curie temperature}} and compares the model magnetic contribution; that contribution is not a simple switch set to zero above the Curie temperature.

image.alt: Cu–Ni FCC and liquid Gibbs energy curves and the pure FCC Ni magnetic energy contribution versus temperature.

Interpret and recover · The magnetic-off run switches off only the magnetic energy term and leaves everything else unchanged. It is a comparison, not a real nonmagnetic alloy. modules.title: Ni–Nb · ordered phases and amount bases

blocks.text: In plain words: Some phases keep each element on its own set of positions, so energies are often given per formula unit instead of per atom. One division converts them; dividing twice is a common mistake. Picture: a box of sites, some only for nickel and some only for niobium.

Cards you may need: [[card#phase-model-state|phase, phase model, grid state]], [[card#f-np|f and NP]], [[card#calphad-database|CALPHAD and databases]], [[card#sigma|what Σ means]], [[card#tdb-line|reading a TDB line]].

Problem · How do ordered phases change the amount basis? This step reads a Ni–Nb calculation made in advance with pycalphad from the database published with Sun et al.’s assessment. Practise the conversion with the given energies before opening the results explorer.

Heads-up: in this step μ and δ are names of two Ni–Nb phases, written {{mu_phase|μ phase}} and {{delta_phase|δ phase}}. They are not the chemical potential {{mu_chem|μ_A}} or the boundary preference {{delta_pref|δ}} from steps 02–04. Hover over or tap any marked symbol to see what it means here.

A sublattice is a group of sites whose allowed occupants and capacity enter the model. An endmember fixes an occupant on each sublattice; it is a model building block, not necessarily a stable material. The [[glossary#compound-energy-formalism-cef|compound energy formalism (CEF)]] combines these building blocks. In the literature the occupancy of each sublattice is written as site fractions $y$; the CEF energy adds the endmember energies weighted by products of site fractions, an ideal mixing term on each sublattice, and excess terms. Here the {{delta_phase|δ phase}} has three sublattices in ratio 1:1:2, four atoms per formula; the {{mu_phase|μ phase}} has five in ratio 2:2:2:6:1, thirteen atoms per formula. The database numbers the sublattices but does not say which crystal sites they are; for the {{mu_phase|μ phase}} the site counts are enough to match most of them, as the sketch below shows. Composition follows from the occupancy: in the ideal NbNi₃ formula of the {{delta_phase|δ phase}}, one of the four sites per formula holds Nb, so $x(\mathrm{Nb}) = 1/4 = 0.25$; click the boxes below to try other fillings. In the 1200 K sample used in the attempt, the {{delta_phase|δ phase}} has $x(\mathrm{Nb}) = 0.2599$, close to that.

The names {{delta_phase|δ}}-NbNi₃ and {{mu_phase|μ}}-Nb₇Ni₆ give the ideal compositions; because sites can hold either element, each phase spans a composition range. pycalphad gives a phase’s energy per mole of formula units ({{g_formula|G_formula}}) or per mole of atoms ({{gm|GM}}).

Approach · Divide a formula-basis energy by its number of atoms per formula, once. Leave GM, which is already per mole of atoms, unchanged. Phase amounts NP are also per mole of atoms, not formula counts. The map’s “mol formula units” setting only recounts the same amount (NP divided by the atoms per formula); balances always use NP itself. A database file also lists a reference enthalpy for each element; that is bookkeeping for the [[glossary#ser|stable element reference]] and is already built into these energies, so do not add it.

Reading the diagram · Here is the saved calculation, read the same way as [[cuni#reading-the-diagram|Cu–Ni in step 05]]: dots are compositions of phases found at one grid temperature, and empty areas between them are two-phase regions. The {{delta_phase|δ phase}} and the {{mu_phase|μ phase}} appear as narrow bands near $x(\mathrm{Nb}) = 0.25$ and at about 0.48–0.59, {{nbni_phase|NbNi₈}} as a thin line near 0.11 at low temperature (a [[glossary#ordered-phase-line-compound|line compound]]), and Nb-rich BCC on the right.

image.alt: Ni–Nb sampled equilibrium phase compositions versus temperature and Nb atom mole fraction, showing liquid, FCC, BCC, delta, mu and NbNi8 fields.

blocks.text: Where the liquid region narrows to a point between two liquid + solid regions, a [[glossary#eutectic|eutectic]] sits at that tip: on cooling, the liquid turns into two solids at one temperature. On the clickable map, try $x(\mathrm{Nb}) \approx 0.40$: liquid alone at 1470 K, {{delta_phase|δ}} + {{mu_phase|μ}} one row below at 1425 K, so a eutectic lies between those temperatures. Another sits near 0.16, where liquid at 1560 K gives FCC + {{delta_phase|δ}} at 1515 K. In a binary at fixed pressure, [[glossary#three-phases-at-one-temperature|three phases can coexist only at a single temperature]], so this 45 K grid never lands exactly on it. After your attempt, the results explorer shows the calculation as a [[ninb/lab/map|clickable map]], with amounts in mol atoms or in mol formula units.

Attempt · Convert the two supplied energies to J/mol atoms. Why would dividing the per-atom energy ({{gm|GM}}) by four or thirteen again be wrong? At the supplied 1200 K sample, overall $x(\mathrm{Nb}) = 0.3416$: the {{mu_phase|μ phase}} has atom-mole fraction 0.3705990971416999 and $x(\mathrm{Nb}) = 0.48038239728767557$; the {{delta_phase|δ phase}} has fraction 0.6294009028581448 and $x(\mathrm{Nb}) = 0.25988319454193687$. (The calculation was set up for $x(\mathrm{Nb}) = 0.35$, between the {{delta_phase|δ-phase}} and {{mu_phase|μ-phase}} compositions; the calculation used 51 compositions from 0.005 to 0.995, and 0.3416 is the nearest grid point.)

The energy divisor converts one mole of formulas to the corresponding moles of real atoms. That conversion has already occurred for GM and NP; dividing them again would corrupt energies and balances.
