modules.title: From materials science · splits, the Ω bump and a menu

blocks.text: In plain words: The advanced steps ask one question in many ways: how do you know an equilibrium answer is really the lowest? This step gathers what you already know about splits, adds one new picture, a curve that bends down, and lets you pick the cheapest mixture from a short list by hand. Picture: one curve with a hump, touched twice by one straight line.

Cards you may need: [[card#lever-rule|the lever rule]], [[card#common-tangent|the common tangent]], [[card#chord-rule|the chord rule]], [[card#metastable-unstable|metastable or unstable]], [[card#parallel-tangent|the parallel tangent]].

Problem · Which mixture of a few listed states is cheapest, and how would you know that nothing lower exists? The sample has overall composition $z$. Three ideas from steps 00–06 carry all of the advanced steps: a split keeps every atom, its energy lies on a straight line, and the best split is a common tangent.

Heads-up: this step prepares steps 10–17 for learners who know CALPHAD from materials science or have worked through steps 00–06. It has three parts: two phases (a recap), one phase model with two phases, and a menu by hand. If you worked through [[twophase|step 03]] parts A–C on this site, skim the first part. All energies are J/mol atoms; $x$ and $z$ are B atom fractions.

blocks.label: Self-check · entry check: can you skip this step?

blocks.text: If you can answer all five, go straight to [[menu|step 10]]. Answers are in the next box.

items: A sample at $z=0.30$ splits into states at $x=0.191$ and $x=0.809$. What fraction is in the second state?
Where on the $g$–$x$ plot does the energy of that split lie?
What are the end heights of the tangent at a point of a curve called?
One curve, touched twice by one straight line: how many phase models, and how many phases?
A uniform sample sits where its curve bends up, but a split would be lower. Stable, metastable or unstable?
On the straight line (the chord) between the two states, at $x=z$.
The chemical potentials $\mu_A$ (at $x=0$) and $\mu_B$ (at $x=1$).
One phase model, two phases of different composition: a miscibility gap.
Metastable: stable against small changes, but not the lowest.

blocks.text: Two phases, a recap · In step 02 one bulk phase had one curve, and the tangent at the sample's composition gave the chemical potentials: its height at $x=0$ is $\mu_A$ and at $x=1$ is $\mu_B$. With two phase models the sample can do better by splitting. Here are step 02's ALPHA and its mirror image BETA at 1000 K. One straight line touches both curves, at $x=0.191$ and $x=0.809$: the common tangent. Its end heights are the chemical potentials of both phases, $-10762.7$ J/mol here, the same in both: that is why they can coexist.

A split's energy per mole of atoms of the sample is $G=f_1g_1+f_2g_2$, so drawn on the plot it lies on the straight line between its two points, at $x=z$: the chord rule. The amounts come from keeping every atom, $f_1+f_2=1$ and $f_1x_1+f_2x_2=z$: the lever rule, which you met in [[twophase#attempt|step 03]]. At $z=0.30$ the split has $f_{\mathrm{BETA}}=(0.30-0.191)/(0.809-0.191)\approx0.176$.

image.alt: ALPHA and BETA curves at 1000 K with one straight line touching ALPHA at x = 0.191 and BETA at x = 0.809, and a dotted line at z = 0.30

blocks.text: Remember the solid–liquid fraction line of step 01? There the computer already chose the amounts of two states, non-negative and adding to one. The advanced steps do the same with many more candidates. The melting lens of step 03 part C draws the compositions of coexisting solid and liquid at every temperature. At 1400 K the tie line runs from liquid at 0.312 to solid at 0.441, and a sample at $z=0.40$ is about 0.68 solid. Steps 10–14 use exactly this case.

image.alt: The melting lens between 1000 K and 1800 K, with the tie line at 1400 K from 0.312 to 0.441 and z = 0.40 marked on it

blocks.text: One phase model, two phases · Now take only one phase model: step 02's ALPHA with an extra energy for unlike neighbours, $\Omega x(1-x)$ with $\Omega=20000$ J/mol, at 800 K. This is [[twophase#part-b-one-phase-model-two-phases|step 03 part B]]'s regular solution. Its curve has a hump: in the middle it bends down. One straight line touches the same curve twice, at 0.070 and 0.930. A sample in between splits into an A-rich and a B-rich region with the same crystal structure: one phase model, two phases, a miscibility gap.

The picture shows $g$ minus its straight end line, which moves no touching point and makes the hump easy to see. The bends matter. Where the curve bends up, a uniform sample is stable against small composition changes. Between 0.070 and the point where the bending changes sign, 0.211, it is still stable against small changes, but a split is lower: metastable. Between 0.211 and 0.789 the curve bends down and any small change lowers the energy: unstable. The touching points 0.070 and 0.930 are the binodal, the bending points 0.211 and 0.789 the spinodal.

image.alt: The regular solution at 800 K drawn as g minus its straight end line: a hump in the middle and one flat tangent touching at 0.070 and 0.930

blocks.text: A metastable alloy can stay as it is for a long time: forming the new region needs a small nucleus, which costs interface energy, and atoms must move. Real alloys do this. The Cu–Ni database of [[cuni|step 05]] has a low-temperature miscibility gap in FCC, and supersaturated solid solutions are a standard starting point for heat treatments.

One more picture you met in [[boundary#where-the-odds-formula-comes-from|step 04]]: the parallel tangent. Take the tangent at the alloy's own composition and slide it down, keeping its tilt, until it touches the curve again. How far it moved is the bulk driving force for forming that other composition. Step 14 uses the same move for its floor, a guaranteed lower limit on the energy.

At $z=0.15$ (between 0.070 and 0.211) the regular solution at 800 K is metastable: the curve bends up there, but the split at 0.070 and 0.930 is lower. At $z=0.50$ it is unstable: the curve bends down, with a curvature of about $-13.4$ kJ/mol atoms, so any small change lowers the energy and there is no barrier at all in this bulk model.

blocks.label: Dive deeper · nucleus, interface and a real example (about 5 min)

blocks.text: The parallel tangent gives a bulk driving force per mole. A real nucleus also has to pay for its interface and often for elastic strain, so the composition that grows first is not simply where the bulk gain is largest. Iron–chromium steels show a well-known case: a ferrite separates into iron-rich and chromium-rich regions near 475 °C, which makes the steel brittle.

Approach · A program cannot draw a smooth curve. It works with a list of candidate states, each one phase model at one composition: a dot on the $g$–$x$ plot. The advanced steps call such a list a menu. A sample at $z$ can be made from any two dots on either side of $z$; the lever rule gives their amounts, and the chord rule gives the energy. The best mixture of the menu is the lowest chord above $z$.

Attempt · Four dots from the ALPHA/BETA pair at 1000 K: ALPHA at 0.2 ($-10760.596$), ALPHA at 0.4 ($-9795.756$), BETA at 0.6 ($-9795.756$) and BETA at 0.8 ($-10760.596$ J/mol atoms). The sample has $z=0.35$.

items: Which pairs of dots can make $z=0.35$? (One dot must lie on each side.)
For each pair, find the amounts with the lever rule and the energy of the mixture.
Which pair is cheapest? Compare it with the uniform ALPHA at $z=0.35$, $-10183.195$ J/mol atoms.
The true split of step 03 uses 0.191 and 0.809 and reaches $-10762.730$. Why is your best menu answer higher?

blocks.text: Only ALPHA at 0.2 lies left of 0.35, so every pair uses it. Its partner is one of the three dots to the right.
For the partner at $x_2$: $f_2=(0.35-0.2)/(x_2-0.2)$ and $f_1=1-f_2$. The energy is $f_1\times(-10760.596)+f_2\times g_2$.

The cheapest pair is ALPHA at 0.2 with BETA at 0.8, 0.75 and 0.25, at $-10760.596$ J/mol atoms, well below the uniform ALPHA ($-10183.195$). It is still 2.134 above the true split, because the menu has no dot at 0.191 or 0.809: a menu answer can never be lower than the truth, and it is only as good as its dots. That difference between a menu answer and the truth is what the advanced steps are about.

Explore · Open [[from-materials/lab/omega|the Ω bump]] and raise $\Omega/RT$: above 2 the curve bends down, one line touches it twice, and the metastable and unstable bands appear; the regular solution of steps 15–17 sits at about 3. Then open [[twophase/lab/part-d|part D of the step 03 lab]] and play the grid method with a coarse grid: a correct calculation can still miss the split.

Interpret · Everything in this step is an invented teaching model: no real alloy, no interface energy and no kinetics. What carries over is the method. A split is a chord, the best split is a tangent, chemical potentials are its end heights, and a calculation that only knows a list of dots can only be as good as its dots.

blocks.label: Dive deeper · the menu in symbols (about 5 min)

blocks.text: Number the dots $j=1,2,\dots$; dot $j$ has composition $x_j$ and energy $g_j$. Choose amounts $f_j\ge0$ with $\sum_j f_j=1$ and $\sum_j f_jx_j=z$, and make $\sum_j f_jg_j$ as small as possible. The symbol $\sum_j$ means "add up over all dots". This is a linear programme: once the dots are fixed, the total energy and both balances are straight-line functions of the amounts $f_j$. The curves $g(x)$ themselves are not straight; only the amounts are chosen. The optional [[lp-primer|LP primer]] explains linear programmes from scratch.

Next · [[menu|Step 10]], where both starting points meet, begins with a grid that misses the split, and turns your menu into the problem a computer solves. Never met a linear programme? Read the optional [[lp-primer|LP primer]] first (about an hour).

modules.title: From operations research · energy, phases and cost curves

blocks.text: In plain words: At fixed temperature and pressure, a closed sample's equilibrium is its allowed state of lowest G: energy minus temperature times an entropy bonus. Each phase model gives a cost curve per mole of atoms, a straight line plus a term from counting arrangements. Picture: two cost curves on [0, 1], one possibly not convex.
Cards you may need: [[card#why-min-g|why minimise G]], [[card#h-and-s|H and S]], [[card#mole-atoms|z, x and f]], [[card#ideal-g|building g(x)]], [[card#regular-omega|what Ω does]].

Problem · What is the objective function of a materials equilibrium, and what are its variables and constraints? By the end of this step you can write down the cost of any state of a two-element sample, per mole of atoms, and see why the cost curves can make a split beat every single state.

Heads-up: steps 08 and 09 are for readers who know linear programming, duality and branch-and-bound but no thermodynamics. Together they take about two and a half hours. If you know LP duality and column generation, the self-check at the end of [[or-prices|step 09]] offers a fast path to step 12. All energies are J/mol atoms. The card [[card#lp-names|how this course names LP things]] lists the course's words and signs; the optional LP primer is written for materials readers, and you can skip it.

blocks.label: Self-check · entry check: can you skip this step?

blocks.text: If you can answer all five, go straight to step 09. Answers are in the next box.

items: At fixed temperature and pressure, which quantity does a closed sample minimise at equilibrium?
Is the enthalpy $H$ "the heat stored in the sample"?
A sample at overall B fraction $z=0.40$ is half a state at $x=0.5$ and half a state at $x=0.3$. Does it keep every atom?
You add the same straight line $a+bx$ to every cost curve. Does the cheapest split change?
When does an extra term $\Omega x(1-x)$ make a cost curve non-convex?
The Gibbs energy $G=H-TS$.
No. It is the energy bookkeeping at fixed pressure; in these models mostly bonding energy.
No. Only the prices shift: $\mu_A$ by $a$ and $\Delta\mu$ by $b$ ($\mu_A$ and $\Delta\mu=\mu_B-\mu_A$ are the prices of the two atom balances, the duals; step 09 defines them).
When $\Omega>2RT$ (for a curve built as in this step).

blocks.text: The rule: lowest G · Put a sample with fixed amounts of two elements, A and B, in a large heat bath at temperature $T$ and pressure $p$. Heat may cross; atoms may not. The second law says that the entropy of sample plus bath cannot fall. At fixed $T$ and $p$, with only pressure–volume work, that is the same as "the Gibbs energy $G$ of the sample cannot rise". So at equilibrium the closed sample minimises $G=H-TS$ among its allowed states. Whether and how fast a real sample gets there is kinetics, not the second law: a function that cannot rise does not by itself reach its global minimum.

items: $H$, the enthalpy, is the energy bookkeeping at fixed pressure, here mostly bonding energy. It is not "stored heat".
$S$, the entropy, counts arrangements: $S=k_B\ln W$ for $W$ microscopic arrangements of the whole sample. Per mole of atoms it is $R\ln W/N$ for $N$ atoms.
$-TS$ is an entropy bonus. Optimisation reading: a scalarised two-objective problem, low $H$ and high $S$, with $T$ as the weight.
One number: pure A at 1400 K has $g=1000-10\times1400=-13000$ as a solid and $7000-16\times1400=-15400$ J/mol as a liquid, so the liquid wins.

blocks.label: Dive deeper · the second law in three lines (about 5 min)

blocks.text: Let the sample take heat $Q$ from the bath. The bath's entropy falls by $Q/T$, and at fixed $p$ with only $pV$ work, $Q=\Delta H$ of the sample. The second law says $\Delta S-\Delta H/T\ge0$ for the sample plus bath. Multiply by $-T$: $\Delta H-T\Delta S=\Delta G\le0$. Every allowed change lowers $G$ or keeps it; at equilibrium no allowed change can lower it further.

Phase model, phase and amounts · A phase model, for example SOLID or LIQUID, is a formula for one structure that gives a cost curve $g(x)$, in J per mole of atoms. A phase is a uniform region of a real sample; several coexisting phases can share one phase model. The variables of the problem are amounts: $f_j$ is the moles of atoms in state $j$ per mole of sample. A state $j$ has its own B fraction $x_j$; the whole sample has the fixed overall B fraction $z$. Energies per mole of atoms work like cost per tonne in blending.

Conservation of atoms is the constraint set: $\sum_j f_j=1$ (all atoms are somewhere), $\sum_j f_jx_j=z$ (all B atoms are somewhere), $f_j\ge0$. The A balance follows from the two. The objective is $\sum_j f_jg_j$.

Building one cost curve · Each phase model's curve is a straight line between its two pure ends, $(1-x)g^\circ_A+xg^\circ_B$, plus a mixing term $RT[x\ln x+(1-x)\ln(1-x)]$. The mixing term is $-T$ times the mixing entropy per mole of atoms. Counting the arrangements of $k$ B atoms on $N$ sites gives $\ln W/N\to-[x\ln x+(1-x)\ln(1-x)]$ for large $N$, which is positive: entropy-regularised optimisation, with $R$ converting per-atom counts to per-mole energies. At $x=0.4$ and 1400 K the mixing term is about $-7834$ J/mol atoms.

With $N$ sites and $k$ B atoms, $W=N!/(k!\,(N-k)!)$. Stirling's approximation $\ln n!\approx n\ln n-n$ gives $\ln W\approx N\ln N-k\ln k-(N-k)\ln(N-k)=-N[x\ln x+(1-x)\ln(1-x)]$ with $x=k/N$. For $N=100$ and $k=40$ the exact $\ln W/N$ is about 0.648 and the limit $-[0.4\ln0.4+0.6\ln0.6]$ is 0.673; the two approach each other as $N$ grows.

Reference states · Only differences of $G$ matter. Adding the same straight line $a+bx$ to every phase model's curve leaves every split unchanged; it shifts the price of A by $a$ and the exchange slope by $b$. That is why the numbers are large and negative, and why "zero" is only a chosen reference. In LP terms: adding the same affine function of the constraint rows to every cost changes the optimal value and the duals, not the optimal amounts.

The Ω bump · A regular solution adds $\Omega x(1-x)$ to one phase model's curve: unlike neighbours cost energy. Once $\Omega>2RT$ the curve bends down somewhere: it is no longer convex. With the straight-line tilt of the pure ends, two separate valleys need not be visible in $g$ itself; subtract the end line, or later the price line, and they are. One phase model can then describe two coexisting phases of different composition: a miscibility gap.

Approach · Read the problem as an LP over states. The columns are candidate states (a phase model at one composition), each with cost $g_j$ and rows $(1,x_j)$. The right-hand side is $(1,z)$. The decision is how much of each state to use. Everything that follows is LP theory with a physical meaning for each piece.

Attempt · Use the melting lens at 1400 K: A melts at 1000 K and B at 1800 K. Its pure-end values at 1400 K are $g^\circ_A=-15400$ and $g^\circ_B=-8000$ for LIQUID, $-13000$ and $-12000$ for SOLID (J/mol atoms).

items: Build $g_{\mathrm{LIQUID}}(0.3)$: the end-line value plus the mixing term. Use $RT=11640.3$ J/mol and $0.3\ln0.3+0.7\ln0.7=-0.610864$.
A sample at $z=0.40$ uses only LIQUID at 0.3 and SOLID at 0.5. Find both amounts from the two constraint rows.
Every curve is raised by 1000 J/mol (so $a=1000$, $b=0$). What happens to the best amounts and to the price of A?
The regular solution of step 15 has $\Omega=20000$ J/mol at 800 K, where $2RT\approx13303$ J/mol. Is its curve convex?

blocks.text: End line: $0.7\times(-15400)+0.3\times(-8000)$. The amounts solve $f_L+f_S=1$ and $0.3f_L+0.5f_S=0.40$.
A constant added to every cost adds the same constant to every mixture, whatever the amounts. Compare $\Omega$ with $2RT$.

$g_{\mathrm{LIQUID}}(0.3)=-13180.0+11640.3\times(-0.610864)=-13180.0-7110.6=-20290.6$ J/mol atoms. The amounts are $f_L=f_S=0.5$, because 0.40 lies halfway between 0.3 and 0.5. Raising every curve by 1000 J/mol changes no amount; the price of A rises by 1000 and the exchange slope stays. With $\Omega=20000>13303$ the regular solution is not convex: it bends down near the middle.

Interpret · These cost curves are models: a straight line between measured pure-element values, an exact counting term, and, for real alloys, fitted extra terms. The optimisation on top is exact for the declared model; whether the model fits the material is a separate question that step 17 returns to.

modules.title: Prices and metastability · temperature and μ as prices

blocks.text: In plain words: Equilibrium is a blending problem. The sample may split, so the cheapest attainable cost is the lower convex envelope of the curves, and the line that supports it has the prices of A and B atoms as its end heights. A sample can stay at a local optimum for a long time, and the curves themselves are fitted models. Picture: the envelope with its supporting line.

Cards you may need: [[card#lower-envelope|the lower envelope]], [[card#chemical-potential|chemical potential]], [[card#metastable-unstable|metastable or unstable]], [[card#twin-dots|twin dots]], [[card#calphad-database|CALPHAD and databases]].

Problem · Given the cost curves, what is the cheapest way to make a sample of overall B fraction $z$, and which prices support that answer? And when is a sample that is not at the cheapest state still stuck where it is?

Heads-up: this step closes the thermodynamics for readers from operations research. Its last part is a three-question self-check; if you pass it, the short summary below lets you skip steps 10 and 11 and the first part of step 12.

blocks.label: Self-check · entry check: can you skip this step?

blocks.text: If you can answer all five, go to the self-check at the end of this step. Answers are in the next box.

items: Why can a mixture of two states be cheaper than every single state at the same $z$?
At the melting point, how do the solid and liquid lines of a pure element compare?
Where on the $g$–$x$ plot do you read the chemical potentials $\mu_A$ and $\mu_B$ of a state?
A uniform state where the curve bends up, but with a cheaper split available: what is it called?
Where do the cost curves of a real alloy come from?
Its cost lies on the chord between the two states; where the curves are not convex, or where two curves cross, a chord lies below the curves.
They cross: the same $g$ at that temperature.
As the end heights of the tangent at that state: at $x=0$ and at $x=1$.
Metastable.
From a CALPHAD database: physics-based formulas with parameters fitted to data.

blocks.text: Mixtures beat single states · A split's cost is the amount-weighted sum of its parts, so on the plot it lies on the chord between the two states. The cheapest cost reachable at each $z$ is the lower convex envelope of all the curves. Where the envelope is straight, it touches two states, and a sample there splits into spatially separate regions with those compositions, in amounts given by the lever rule. The model leaves out the energy of the interfaces between the regions. So a mixture of listed states is always a real arrangement, and its energy is a ceiling for the truth; a state the list leaves out can be lower. On a grid, two neighbouring dots of the same phase model often stand for one phase between them, not two phases; but inside a miscibility gap two dots of one phase model can be two real compositions of a split. The curve between them decides.

Temperature moves the curves · Each pure-end value is a straight line in temperature, $g^\circ=h-Ts$. For pure A, the solid line $1000-10T$ and the liquid line $7000-16T$ cross at 1000 K: the melting point. Above it the liquid is cheaper. Every curve in $x$ moves as $T$ changes, so the envelope and its touching points move too.

blocks.label: Dive deeper · tie line, liquidus, solidus and the lens (about 10 min)

blocks.text: At each temperature the common tangent of SOLID and LIQUID touches at two compositions. Joined on a temperature–composition plot they form a tie line; their traces over all temperatures are the liquidus (liquid side) and the solidus (solid side), and between them lies the lens. At 1400 K the tie line runs from liquid at 0.312 to solid at 0.441. [[unary/lab|The step 01 lab]] shows the crossing of the pure lines and [[twophase/lab/part-c|part C of the step 03 lab]] draws the lens.

Chemical potentials are prices · The chemical potential $\mu_B$ is the change in $G$ per mole of B added, for a small addition at fixed $T$, $p$ and amount of A. On the plot it is a height: the tangent at a state meets $x=0$ at $\mu_A$ and $x=1$ at $\mu_B$, and its slope is the exchange slope of step 02 $\Delta\mu=\mu_B-\mu_A$. For an ideal phase $\mu_B=g^\circ_B+RT\ln x$. Coexisting phases share one tangent, so they share the prices: that is the equilibrium condition. In LP terms the supporting line of the envelope is the dual solution.

Stable, metastable, unstable · Where a curve bends up, a uniform state is stable against small composition changes. The model has no barrier of its own: barriers come from interface energy, which the bulk model leaves out. If a cheaper split exists while the curve still bends up, the state is metastable: optimal against small changes of composition (the curve bends up there), though not against a split into distant compositions, and a real sample can keep it for a long time. Inside the spinodal, where the curve bends down, it is unstable and any small change lowers the cost.

Between the binodal (the touching points of the common tangent) and the spinodal (where the bending changes sign) a uniform state is metastable. The parallel tangent measures by how much: slide the tangent at the state down, keeping its slope, until it touches the curve again; the drop is the largest bulk driving force. A supersaturated solid solution is the classic example: it holds more B than equilibrium allows and splits only after a nucleus forms. In the regular solution at 800 K the binodal is 0.070 and 0.930 and the spinodal 0.211 and 0.789.

CALPHAD · Real cost curves are fitted models stored in a database and extrapolated to compositions and temperatures where no measurement exists. Optimisation reading: the objective coefficients are estimates. A perfectly solved model can still be wrong about the material.

blocks.label: Dive deeper · what goes into a database (about 10 min)

blocks.text: CALPHAD models use physics-based forms: sublattices for ordered crystals, magnetic terms, and lattice stabilities, the energies of pure elements in structures they do not adopt on their own. Parameters are fitted subsystem by subsystem, each element and each binary to its own data, then combined. Metastable phases and extrapolated regions are often only weakly constrained by data.

Approach · Read the lens at 1400 K as an LP over all states of both phase models. Its optimal value as a function of $z$ is the lower envelope; its dual solution is the common tangent. Check the prices, then the amounts, then the cost, and finally use the bending of the regular solution to tell metastable from unstable.
Attempt · The lens at 1400 K has its common tangent at $\mu_A=-19760.0$ and $\Delta\mu=-1782.8$ J/mol atoms. It touches LIQUID at $x=0.312$ and SOLID at $x=0.441$.

0.15 lies between the binodal 0.070 and the spinodal 0.211; 0.50 lies inside the spinodal.

items: Equilibrium is the cheapest mixture of candidate states: an LP whose rows are "amounts add to 1" and "B atoms add to $z$". In step 10's menu of ten states at $z=0.40$, the answer is SOLID at 0.5 and LIQUID at 0.3, half each, at $-20429.54$ J/mol atoms.

The duals form a line $\mu_A+\Delta\mu\,x$ that lies under every menu state: a floor for the menu, equal to the ceiling there (strong duality). Its intercept $\mu_A$ and slope $\Delta\mu$ are the menu's estimates of the chemical potential of A and of the exchange slope: $-19873.9$ and $-1389.0$.

The reduced cost over the continuous curves is the gap curve, $g(x)$ minus the line, and its negative is the driving force. Menu states above the line are unused; the deepest dip below it, $-61.2$ near SOLID 0.4489, is the column to add.

Interpret · You now have the dictionary: amounts are the variables, atom balances the constraints, the Gibbs energy the objective, chemical potentials the duals, and the driving force the negative reduced cost. Every word carries a physical meaning in steps 10–18, and every model there is an invented teaching model.

modules.title: LP primer · the cheapest mix, and how to prove it

blocks.text: In plain words: A linear programme is a recipe for one kind of question: choose some amounts, keep a few rules, and make a total as small as possible. Every total is a sum of amount times a fixed number, as kilograms and euros are. On this page you learn the recipe on a melt-shop question, see how a computer searches, and meet the extra numbers it returns, its prices. Picture: lots of scrap as dots on a price-against-content plot, and a straight line under them.

Cards you may need: [[card#optimisation-anatomy|objective, variables, constraints]], [[card#lever-rule|the lever rule]], [[card#chord-rule|the chord rule]], [[card#line|reading a line]], [[card#sigma|the symbol Σ]].

Problem · A melt shop must make 1 kg of a copper–nickel alloy with exactly 0.40 kg of nickel in it, from the scrap lots in the table, as cheaply as possible. Which lots should it buy, how much of each, and how would it know that no cheaper charge exists?

Heads-up: this page is optional. It prepares [[menu|step 10]] onwards for anyone who has never met a linear programme (LP), and you can read it any time after [[twophase|step 03]]; it takes about an hour without the optional boxes. The prices and contents are invented for the exercise. Amounts here are kilograms and contents are mass fractions; in step 10 they are moles of atoms and atom fractions. The recipe does not mind, as long as one problem keeps one basis throughout.

blocks.label: Self-check · entry check: can you skip this page?

blocks.text: If you can answer all four, go straight to [[menu|step 10]]. Answers are in the next box.

items: In "minimise $c_1f_1+c_2f_2$ subject to $f_1+f_2=1$, $f_1,f_2\ge0$", what may you choose, and what does "subject to" mean?
Two rules (equations) and many candidate amounts: at most how many amounts are non-zero in a best corner answer?
What does a solver's price (dual value) of a rule tell you?
Why can a straight line under all the candidates prove that a choice is the cheapest?
You choose the amounts $f_1$ and $f_2$. "Subject to" means "while keeping these rules".
Two: at most as many as there are rules.
How much the best total changes per unit change of that rule's right-hand side, for small changes, while the same candidates stay in use.
Every candidate costs at least the line's height at its own content, so any mixture costs at least the line's height at the target; if one mixture reaches that height, nothing is cheaper.

blocks.text: You can skip this page. The card [[card#lp-names|how this course names LP things]] lists the words and signs the course uses: amounts $f$ (never $x$, which is a composition here), equality rows, SciPy's marginals as the change of the optimum per unit right-hand side, ceiling and floor for the primal and dual bounds.
Approach · Every linear programme has the same three parts. Say them in plain words first:

items: Choose the amounts $f_j\ge0$ of each lot, in kg (the variables);
to make the total cost $\sum_j f_j\,c_j$ as small as possible (the objective; $c_j$ is lot $j$'s price);
while keeping the rules: the amounts add to 1 kg, $\sum_j f_j=1$, and the nickel adds to 0.40 kg, $\sum_j f_j\,w_j=0.40$ (the constraints).

blocks.text: Books and papers write the same thing in one line: minimise $\sum_j f_jc_j$ subject to $\sum_j f_j=1$, $\sum_j f_jw_j=0.40$, $f_j\ge0$. "Subject to" means "while keeping these rules"; some write "s.t.". A choice that keeps every rule is feasible (possible to make); any feasible choice with the lowest total is optimal. Linear means that the total and every rule are sums of amounts times fixed numbers: double an amount and its cost doubles. The numbers $w_j$ and $c_j$ are fixed data; only the amounts are chosen.

headers: Ni content $w$, kg Ni per kg

blocks.text: You have solved linear programmes before without the name. In [[unary|step 01]] the computer chose the amounts of solid and liquid, non-negative and adding to 1, and the cheaper end won. The lever rule of [[twophase|step 03]] is two rules and two amounts; a negative amount meant "cannot be made". The chord rule says that a mixture's total lies on the straight line between its parts. This page adds one thing: many candidates, and a way to know that none is cheaper.
Attempt · Use the table of lots.

items: Which lots have less nickel than 0.40, and which more? Can CuNi10 and CuNi30 together make 0.40?
Use the lever rule for three charges that make 1 kg at 0.40: Cu with Ni cathode; Cu with Monel; CuNi30 with Monel. What does each cost?
Nine pairs have one lot below 0.40 and one above. Which is the cheapest of all, and how many lots does it use?
The cheapest charge could, in principle, mix three or four lots. Why does it not need to?

blocks.text: With two lots the lever rule fixes the amounts: the share of the richer lot is $(0.40-w_{\text{poor}})/(w_{\text{rich}}-w_{\text{poor}})$. For CuNi10 and CuNi30 this share is 1.5, so the other amount is $-0.5$: impossible.

Draw the lots as dots, price against content. A two-lot charge at 0.40 costs the height of the straight line (the chord) between them at 0.40. The cheapest charge is the chord whose height at 0.40 is lowest.

Cu, CuNi10 and CuNi30 lie below 0.40; Constantan, Monel and Ni cathode above. Two lots on the same side cannot make 0.40: one amount would be negative. The cheapest of the nine pairs is 0.714 kg CuNi30 and 0.286 kg Monel, €8.914 per kg (the other four pairs cost 9.15 to 10.43). It uses two lots and needs no more: a charge of three lots at 0.40 is a mixture of two-lot charges, each at 0.40 (pair each lot below 0.40 with one above), and the cheaper of those costs no more than the mixture. With two rules a best charge never needs more than two lots, although ties can allow more (dive deeper below).

How the computer searches · Trying every pair works for six lots, not for thousands. A solver searches instead. Start from any pair that can make the charge, say copper scrap and nickel cathode. Draw the straight line through those two dots. Every other lot whose dot lies below the line is cheaper than what the line offers at its content: bring in the one furthest below, and drop the used lot on the same side of 0.40 (only that swap keeps both amounts positive). Repeat until no dot lies below the line.

Two swaps instead of nine pairs. This is the (primal) simplex method, the classic LP algorithm, on a two-rule problem: it walks from pair to pair, and the cost never rises. Books call each pair a corner of the set of allowed charges; with six amounts that set cannot be drawn, but the textbook picture below shows corners in a case you can draw. It is the computer's search, not something the metal does.

Prices · When the search stops, the line through the used pair lies under every dot. Its height at $w=0$ is €6.86 and at $w=1$ it is €12.00: in this charge a kilogram of copper is worth €6.86 and a kilogram of nickel €12.00. The nickel cathode costs €15.50, more than its €12.00 worth here, and copper scrap costs €7.40, more than €6.86: both stay unused. The slope, $12.00-6.86=5.14$ € per unit of content, is the price of nickel content: nudge the target from 0.40 to 0.41 and the cheapest charge costs $5.143\times0.01=0.051$ € more, €8.966. This holds while the same two lots stay in use, for any target between 0.30 and 0.65. At 0.30 or 0.65 the target sits on a used lot and the rates left and right differ.

Why the line proves that nothing is cheaper: every lot costs at least the line's height at its own content, $c_j\ge\pi_0+\pi_1w_j$ with $\pi_0=6.86$ and $\pi_1=5.14$ (from step 11 on they are called $\mu_A$ and $\Delta\mu$). A charge costs $\sum_jf_jc_j$, so it costs at least $\sum_jf_j(\pi_0+\pi_1w_j)=\pi_0\times1+\pi_1\times0.40$, because the amounts add to 1 and the nickel to 0.40. That is the line's height at 0.40, $6.857+5.143\times0.40=8.914$ with the prices to three decimals (the chord rule again). Our charge costs exactly that. So the line is a floor, the charge is a ceiling, and they meet. A floor that passes below the best charge at 0.40 still proves something: no charge costs less than its height there.

A new offer · A dealer offers swarf at $w=0.50$ for €9.20. The line's height at 0.50 is €9.43, so the swarf lies €0.23 below it: it is worth buying. With it, half CuNi30 and half swarf cost €8.80. Checking one new candidate against the line, without solving again, is called pricing; [[column-generation|step 13]] uses it to find missing states.

The textbook picture · Books draw LPs differently, and you will meet this picture everywhere. Take only two lots, CuNi30 (amount $f_P$) and Monel offcuts (amount $f_Q$), and put the amounts on the two axes. Each rule is a straight line that cuts the plane into an allowed and a forbidden side. The rules are now "at least" and "at most", as melt shops often have them:

items: the charge weighs at least 1 kg: $f_P+f_Q\ge1$;
it holds at least 0.40 kg nickel: $0.30f_P+0.65f_Q\ge0.40$;
it holds at most 0.012 kg iron (CuNi30 has 0.6 % iron, Monel 2.0 %): $0.006f_P+0.020f_Q\le0.012$;
the furnace holds at most 1.5 kg: $f_P+f_Q\le1.5$; and no amount is negative.

blocks.text: The allowed charges form a polygon with five corners. The cost $8.40f_P+10.20f_Q$ is constant along straight lines; slide such a cost line towards lower cost until it is about to leave the polygon. It last touches a corner: $f_P=0.714$, $f_Q=0.286$, €8.914, where the weight and nickel rules are tight (kept with equality). It is the same charge as the dots found. If a best answer exists, a best corner always exists. When the cost line lies along an edge, the whole edge ties: at a Monel price of €8.40, or of €18.20.

A rule's price is how much the best cost changes when the number on its right-hand side moves by one unit (1 kg more charge, 1 kg more nickel). Rules with room to spare have price zero: the iron and furnace rules are not tight, and loosening them a little saves nothing. The weight rule costs €6.86 per kg, the nickel rule €5.14 per kg of nickel, the same numbers as the line under the dots. Why 5.14 and not the €12.00 a kilogram of nickel is worth? Asking for 0.01 kg more nickel in the same weight swaps 0.01 kg of copper (worth €6.86) for nickel (worth €12.00): $12.00-6.86=5.14$ per kg of nickel. The nickel price holds for requirements between 0.30 and 0.45 kg. Above 0.45 kg the iron cap takes over from the weight rule: the charge must grow beyond 1 kg, the weight rule has room to spare, and the nickel price jumps (to €50.86 per kg). If both tight rules were exact ("= 1 kg", "= 0.40 kg"), the polygon would shrink to that one corner: the lever rule. If the iron cap were 0.005 kg, no charge would keep every rule; the problem is then infeasible, and a solver says so instead of giving an answer.
Attempt · Use the rules above. Find all five corners of the polygon, which two rules are tight at each, and the cost there. Check that the cheapest is the corner named above.
For the corner where the weight and nickel rules meet, solve $f_P+f_Q=1$ and $0.30f_P+0.65f_Q=0.40$: the lever rule.
Every corner keeps at least two rules tight (here exactly two), because boundary lines meet there. The cheapest is $(0.714,0.286)$.

Explore · Open [[lp-primer/lab/chords|dots and chords]] and put lots in your basket: the lab mixes them by the lever rule and refuses impossible pairs. [[lp-primer/lab/swap|One swap at a time]] runs the search above, round by round, with the line and each lot's distance to it. [[lp-primer/lab/nudge|Move the target]] slides the target content and shows the best cost and its price. [[lp-primer/lab/polygon|The textbook picture]] has the polygon, a cost line you can turn with the Monel price, and the strict iron cap. On paper: the printable LP primer sheet has most of the exercises.
Same problem, new names · Step 10 asks the same question about a sample's energy instead of a charge's cost. Rename two columns and the recipe, the search and the prices carry over:

rows: a state: one phase model at one composition, a dot on the $g$–$x$ plot
nickel content $w$, kg Ni per kg
amounts $f$, kg per kg of charge
amounts $f$, mol atoms per mol of sample
all atoms and all B atoms are kept: $\sum_jf_j=1$, $\sum_jf_jx_j=z$
cheapest mixture of the menu (the ceiling)
worth of 1 kg Cu and of 1 kg Ni
a lot's distance above the line
a new offer below the line
a missing state found by pricing (step 13)

blocks.text: One difference matters. Costs add because lots are bought and melted separately. A mixture of menu dots adds energies the same way: it is a real sample made of separate regions, one for each dot used (the energy of the boundaries between them is ignored). So the true equilibrium is at or below it: the menu's cheapest mixture is a ceiling. It need not be the truth, because the states between the dots are missing: if the atoms of two dots of the same phase model form one phase at the average composition, its energy lies on that phase's curve, which can lie below the chord. That is why the advanced steps keep asking which states the menu left out.

Interpret · A solver ends in one of three ways: optimal (a best answer), infeasible (no choice keeps every rule) or unbounded (the total can fall without limit; a charge cannot, because amounts are never negative and add to 1). At a tie, "optimal" comes with just one of the best answers. An optimal answer is the best of the candidates it was given. The swarf was cheaper than anything on the list, and no solver could have found it without being offered it.
Think it over: which number would the melt shop most like to know before buying a new lot, and where on this page does it come from?

blocks.label: Dive deeper · the general form, and reading SciPy's answer (about 10 min)

blocks.text: The general form is: minimise $c\cdot f$ subject to $A_{\text{eq}}f=b_{\text{eq}}$, $A_{\text{ub}}f\le b_{\text{ub}}$, $f\ge0$. Each row of $A$ is one rule, each column one candidate; $b$ holds the right-hand sides. An "at least" rule is multiplied by $-1$ to become "at most". The room left in an "at most" rule is its slack: zero when the rule is tight.

SciPy's linprog returns res.status (0 optimal, 2 infeasible, 3 unbounded; other codes mean the solver stopped early, so read res.message), res.x (the amounts, despite the name: in this course $x$ is a composition), res.fun (the best total), res.slack, and the prices in res.eqlin.marginals and res.ineqlin.marginals. SciPy's prices are the change of the best total per unit increase of a right-hand side. For a rule multiplied by $-1$ the sign flips, and other solvers may use the opposite sign: check it once with a nudge. The notebook for this page (f4p) does all of this.

blocks.label: Dive deeper · the companion problem about prices (about 10 min)

blocks.text: Every LP has a companion problem, its dual. Here it asks: of all straight lines $\pi_0+\pi_1w$ that stay below every lot, $\pi_0+\pi_1w_j\le c_j$, which is highest at the target, maximise $\pi_0+0.40\,\pi_1$? The argument above shows that any such line is a floor for every charge (weak duality). The highest one meets the cheapest charge (strong duality), and its two numbers are the prices. A lot strictly above the best line is never used; a used lot sits on the line (complementary slackness).

blocks.label: Dive deeper · ties, and prices that are not unique (about 5 min)

blocks.text: Two different things can fail to be unique. Amounts: when the cost line lies along an edge, every point of the edge is optimal (the Monel price €8.40). Prices: when the target sits exactly on a used lot (target 0.30 or 0.65), many lines touch the dots there, the slopes left and right of the target differ (3.33 and 5.14 at 0.30), and two solvers can return different prices for the same best charge. This matters when the list is short. With only Cu and Monel on the list and the target at 0.65, the best charge is 1 kg Monel, and a solver may return the line through Cu and Monel. CuNi30 lies 0.29 below that line, yet 1 kg Monel is already the cheapest charge of all six lots. So with a target on a used lot, a lot below the returned line does not prove that the charge can be improved. Step 10's box on step 03 part D's grid and step 15 meet this again.

blocks.label: Dive deeper · at most as many lots as rules, and the phase rule (about 5 min)

blocks.text: A corner answer uses at most as many candidates as there are equality rules. In step 10 there are two balances, so the cheapest mixture of a menu uses at most two dots, which looks like the phase rule for two components at fixed temperature and pressure. It is only a resemblance: at a tie more dots can be used, and two neighbouring dots of the same phase model can be one phase. The LP does not prove the phase rule.

blocks.label: Check · the primer in five questions

items: Make 2 kg of solder with at least 1.2 kg of tin, from alloy A (0.5 tin, €20 per kg) and alloy B (0.7 tin, €26 per kg), as cheaply as possible. Name the variables, the objective and the rules, then solve it.
In the textbook picture, Monel costs €8.00 instead of €10.20. Which corner is cheapest now, and what does it cost?
Predict the cheapest cost of 1 kg at a target of 0.42 from the price of nickel content. Is the prediction valid?
Is the line with height €6.50 at $w=0$ and slope 5.00 a floor for the six lots? What does it prove about every charge at 0.40?
A solver reports status 2. What does it mean, and which setting of the textbook picture shows it?

blocks.label: Answers · the primer in five questions

items: Variables: $f_A,f_B\ge0$ kg. Objective: $20f_A+26f_B$, as small as possible. Rules: $f_A+f_B=2$ and $0.5f_A+0.7f_B\ge1.2$. With $f_A=2-f_B$ the tin rule gives $f_B\ge1$, so the best is $f_A=f_B=1$, €46.
$(0.571,0.429)$, where the weight and iron rules are tight: $8.40\times0.571+8.00\times0.429=8.23$ €. The corner $(0.714,0.286)$ now costs 8.29.
$8.914+5.14\times0.02=9.017$ € per kg; valid, because 0.42 lies between 0.30 and 0.65, so CuNi30 and Monel stay in use.
Yes: every lot lies above it (by 0.40 to 4.00). So every charge at 0.40 costs at least $6.50+5.00\times0.40=8.50$ €. The cheapest costs 8.91; this floor leaves a remaining uncertainty of 0.41.
Infeasible: no choice keeps every rule. The strict iron cap of 0.005 kg leaves no allowed polygon.

blocks.text: Next · [[menu|Step 10]] uses the same recipe on ten states of the melting lens: you will choose phase amounts instead of scrap, and the prices turn out to be chemical potentials.

modules.title: Menu · equilibrium as the cheapest mixture of listed states

blocks.text: In plain words: A calculation can be correct and still miss the answer, because it can only choose among the states it was given. On this step you list ten candidate states, pick the cheapest mixture that makes your sample, and see how far it lands from the truth. Picture: ten dots on two curves, two of them joined by a straight line.

Cards you may need: [[card#which-model|which model this is]], [[card#lever-rule|the lever rule]], [[card#chord-rule|the chord rule]], [[card#optimisation-anatomy|objective, variables, constraints]], [[card#phase-model-state|phase, phase model, grid state]].

Problem · How can a correct calculation miss a split? [[twophase#part-d-from-scratch-and-with-pycalphad|Step 03 part D]]'s coarse grid, with compositions 0.2, 0.4, 0.6 and 0.8 for both phase models (so the sample sits exactly on the SOLID dot at 0.4), says that a sample at $z=0.40$ is a single SOLID, at $-20434.06$ J/mol atoms. The true answer is a split, 39.1 J/mol atoms lower, at $-20473.12$.

Heads-up: model in steps 10–14: the melting lens of step 03 part C at 1400 K, a sample of overall B fraction $z=0.40$, phase models SOLID and LIQUID (A melts at 1000 K, this B at 1800 K). Energies are J/mol atoms. New to linear programmes? The optional [[lp-primer|LP primer]] starts from scratch.

The menu · Work as the computer does. It cannot use a smooth curve; it gets a list of candidate states, each one phase model at one composition. Here is the menu used from now on: five dots per phase model, at 0.1, 0.3, 0.5, 0.7 and 0.9. The sample's composition 0.40 is not on it.

Approach · Choose amounts $f\ge0$ of the dots so that they add to 1 and their B atoms add to $z=0.40$, and make the total energy as small as possible. With two dots, one on each side of 0.40, the lever rule fixes the amounts, and the chord rule says the energy lies on the straight line between the dots. Try pairs and keep the lowest.

This is the lever-rule bookkeeping of step 03 and of step 07, with ten candidates instead of two. The computer answers the same question as you. A solver does not try every pair, though. The [[lp-primer|LP primer]] shows one search: bring in a dot that lies below the line through the used pair, one swap at a time, until none is left below. Step 11 shows the mirror image: keep a line under every dot and move it until it touches two dots on either side of $z$; SciPy's highs-ds (dual simplex) works this second way.

An LP over candidate states: $\min\sum_jf_jg_j$ subject to $\sum_jf_j=1$, $\sum_jf_jx_j=z$, $f\ge0$. Two equality rows, so a basic optimal solution uses at most two states. The columns are the ten dots.
Attempt · Use the table above.

items: Which dots lie left of 0.40, and which right of it?
Find the energy of three mixtures that make $z=0.40$: LIQUID 0.3 with SOLID 0.5; SOLID 0.3 with SOLID 0.5; LIQUID 0.3 with LIQUID 0.5.
The computer's answer for the whole menu is one of these. Which, and how far is it above the truth, $-20473.12$?
This menu does worse than step 03 part D's single SOLID at 0.40 ($-20434.06$). Why, although it has more dots?

blocks.text: All three pairs have one dot at 0.3 and one at 0.5, and 0.40 is halfway: the amounts are 0.5 and 0.5, so the energy is the average of the two dot energies.
Look at what each grid contains. Does either grid have a dot at exactly 0.40? Does either have a dot near the true compositions, liquid at 0.312 and solid at 0.441?

The computer's answer is LIQUID at 0.3 and SOLID at 0.5, half each, at $-20429.54$ J/mol atoms: 43.6 above the truth. It is even 4.5 above part D's single SOLID. Part D's grid happened to contain the sample's own composition, 0.40, and a single state there is already close to the truth; this menu does not, and neither of its dots is near the true compositions 0.312 and 0.441. A menu answer is only as good as its dots.

blocks.label: Dive deeper · why part D's grid hides the price line (about 5 min)

blocks.text: On part D's grid the sample sits exactly on a used dot, SOLID at 0.40. Many straight lines can touch the dots there, so the price line is not unique: it can rotate about that dot. The energy is still unique. The card [[card#non-uniqueness|what if the answer is not unique?]] has the two kinds of non-uniqueness; step 11 reads the line.

Explore · Open [[menu/lab/menu|the menu builder]] and put dots in your basket: the lab mixes them at $z=0.40$ with the lever rule. Find the cheapest pair, then switch on part D's coarse grid and the curves. On paper: join LIQUID 0.3 and SOLID 0.5 with a straight line and mark its height at 0.40; every other pair that brackets 0.40 lies higher there.

Interpret · The menu's best mixture is a real mixture: the truth can only be at or below it. Call it the ceiling. With a fixed menu nothing tells you how far above the truth the ceiling is; the next steps find a way to measure that.
Think it over: if you could add one more dot to this menu, where would you put it, and why there?
Next · Step 11 asks what else the computer returns: two numbers that turn out to be the chemical potentials.

modules.title: Price line · floor, ceiling and μ under the dots

blocks.text: In plain words: Lay a ruler under the dots and lift it as high as it goes at your sample's composition. Every mixture of these dots lies on or above it, so the ruler is a floor and your best mixture a ceiling. The ruler's end heights are this menu's prices μA and μB. Picture: a ruler resting on two dots.

Cards you may need: [[card#line|reading a line]], [[card#floor-ceiling|floor and ceiling]], [[card#shadow-price|dual or shadow price]], [[card#exchange-potential|the exchange slope]], [[card#slope-derivative|slope and derivative]].
Problem · Besides the amounts, the solver of step 10 returns two numbers. What are they, what do they mean, and what do they promise?

Heads-up: model in steps 10–14: the melting lens of step 03 part C at 1400 K, a sample of overall B fraction $z=0.40$, phase models SOLID and LIQUID (A melts at 1000 K, this B at 1800 K). Energies are J/mol atoms. The [[lp-primer#prices|LP primer's prices]] show the same idea on a melt-shop charge.

The line under the dots · Draw the straight line through the two dots the menu uses, LIQUID at 0.3 ($-20290.64$) and SOLID at 0.5 ($-20568.44$). Its slope is $\Delta\mu=(-20568.44+20290.64)/0.2=-1389.0$ and its height at $x=0$ is $\mu_A=-20290.64+1389.0\times0.3=-19873.9$ J/mol atoms. Every other dot of the menu lies on or above this line.

That makes the line a floor. Any mixture of the menu's dots lies on a chord between dots, and every chord lies on or above a line that is under all the dots. So no mixture of these dots can be lower than the line's height at $z$, which is $-20429.54$. The best mixture of step 10 is a ceiling at exactly the same height: floor and ceiling meet, and the menu is solved. The floor holds for these dots only: a state between them can still lie lower.
A line under every dot that touches the used dots is exactly a common tangent, for a menu instead of curves. Its end heights are the chemical potentials, as for the tangent of step 02.

The two numbers are the duals of the two rows, $(\pi_0,\pi_1)=(\mu_A,\Delta\mu)$. A dual-feasible line is one under all dots (weak duality: a floor); the optimal one meets the primal (strong duality). The basis has two columns, so the duals come from two equations: the line passes through both used dots.

Reading the line · The line's height at $x=0$ is $\mu_A$, at $x=1$ it is $\mu_B=\mu_A+\Delta\mu=-21262.9$, and its slope $\Delta\mu=\mu_B-\mu_A$ is the exchange slope of step 02, read here as a price: the energy of replacing A by B. These are this menu's prices, not yet the prices of the continuous curves; step 13 shows how they change. The second number has a direct meaning: nudge $z$ from 0.40 to 0.41 and the cheapest energy changes by $\Delta\mu\times0.01=-13.9$ J/mol atoms. This holds while the same two dots stay in use, here for any $z$ strictly between 0.3 and 0.5 (step 12; at 0.3 or 0.5 the sample sits on a dot and the line can rotate).
Approach · Find the line from the two used dots, check that it lies under the unused dots, then read its end heights and use it to predict a small change of $z$.
Attempt · Use the menu of step 10, now for a sample at $z=0.60$. Its cheapest mixture is 0.5 of SOLID 0.5 ($-20568.44$) and 0.5 of SOLID 0.7 ($-19410.64$).

items: Compute $\Delta\mu$, $\mu_A$ and $\mu_B$ of the line through these two used dots.
How far above this line are LIQUID at 0.5 ($-19768.44$) and SOLID at 0.3 ($-19810.64$)?
Predict the cheapest energy at $z=0.61$ from the line, and check it with the lever rule on the same two dots.
Both used dots are SOLID. Are they two phases? What does the true curve say at $z=0.60$ (SOLID at 0.6: $-20234.06$)?

blocks.text: The slope is the rise from 0.5 to 0.7 divided by 0.2; then $\mu_A=g(0.5)-0.5\,\Delta\mu$. The line's height at $x$ is $\mu_A+\Delta\mu\,x$.
At $z=0.61$ the lever rule gives 0.45 of SOLID 0.5 and 0.55 of SOLID 0.7. For the last question, see the card [[card#twin-dots|twin dots]].

$\Delta\mu=(-19410.64+20568.44)/0.2=5789.0$, $\mu_A=-20568.44-0.5\times5789.0=-23462.9$ and $\mu_B=-17673.9$ J/mol atoms; the cheapest energy at 0.60 is $-19989.54$. LIQUID at 0.5 lies $-19768.44-(-20568.44)=800.0$ above the line; SOLID at 0.3 lies $-19810.64-(-23462.9+1736.7)=1915.6$ above it. At $z=0.61$ the line gives $-19989.54+57.89=-19931.65$; the lever rule gives $0.45\times(-20568.44)+0.55\times(-19410.64)=-19931.65$, the same. The two SOLID dots are twin dots: they stand for one solid between them, not two phases. The sample at 0.60 lies beyond the lens (which ends at 0.441), so the truth is one SOLID at 0.60, $-20234.06$: 244.5 J/mol atoms below the menu's answer. The line is the menu's, not the curve's.

blocks.label: Dive deeper · the menu's prices and the true ones (about 5 min)

blocks.text: The common tangent of the continuous curves at 1400 K has $\mu_A=-19760.0$ and $\Delta\mu=-1782.8$ J/mol atoms. The menu's line differs from it by more than 100 J/mol in $\mu_A$ and almost 400 in $\Delta\mu$: coarse dots give coarse prices.

blocks.label: Dive deeper · a line that can rotate (about 5 min)

blocks.text: If the sample sits exactly on a used dot at a corner of the lower envelope, as on step 03 part D's grid in step 10, the line can rotate about that dot and stay under every other dot. The energy is unique; $\mu_A$ and $\Delta\mu$ are not, and two solver methods may return different lines. If instead a third dot lies exactly on the line and $z$ lies strictly between the outermost dots on it, the line is unique but the amounts are not: several mixtures of the touching dots make $z$ at the same energy. (In step 01, at the melting point, every solid–liquid split ties in the same way.)

blocks.label: Dive deeper for operations research · the dual problem and the two-by-two solve (about 10 min)

blocks.text: The dual of the menu LP is $\max\ \mu_A+\Delta\mu\,z$ subject to $\mu_A+\Delta\mu\,x_j\le g_j$ for every dot: the highest line under all dots, read at $z$. At the optimum the constraints of the two used dots are tight, so $\mu_A+0.3\Delta\mu=-20290.64$ and $\mu_A+0.5\Delta\mu=-20568.44$: two equations, two unknowns, no matrix inverse needed. Complementary slackness: the slack of a dot's constraint is its gap to the line, and only dots with zero slack can be used.

Explore · Open [[price-line/lab/line|the lab, A line under the dots]]. Make the line a floor, raise it at $z$ as far as it goes, and predict which dots it touches and the value of $\mu_A$. Then press Check: the lab lifts your line until it touches a dot and turns it from dot to dot until two touching dots lie on opposite sides of 0.40. Switch on the true common tangent to compare prices.

Interpret · The solver's extra numbers are physical: the chemical potentials of A and B, and the exchange slope, for the declared menu. They also give a promise: no mixture of these dots can be lower than the line.
Think it over: the menu's $\Delta\mu$ is $-1389.0$, the continuous one $-1782.8$. Which would you report as "the chemical potential difference of this alloy", and why?
Next · Step 12 subtracts the line from every energy and looks at what remains: the gap curve.

modules.title: Gap curve · how far each state lies above or below the line

blocks.text: In plain words: Subtract the line from every energy and the picture flattens: used dots sit at zero, unused dots above it. Do the same for the whole curves and you see where the line is too high, because the curves dip below zero between the dots. Picture: the gap curve, a wavy line around zero.

Cards you may need: [[card#reduced-cost|reduced cost]], [[card#driving-force|driving force]], [[card#raw-grid-line|why the grid line is no floor]], [[card#common-tangent|common tangent]], [[card#lens-curves|liquidus, solidus, lens]].
Problem · Which states does the line say are unused, and which missing state would lower the energy if you added it?

Heads-up: model in steps 10–14: the melting lens of step 03 part C at 1400 K, a sample of overall B fraction $z=0.40$, phase models SOLID and LIQUID (A melts at 1000 K, this B at 1800 K). Energies are J/mol atoms.
The gap curve · For every state, subtract the line's height from its energy: $\mathrm{gap}(x)=g(x)-(\mu_A+\Delta\mu\,x)$. At the menu's dots the gaps are:

Used dots sit at zero; every other dot lies above the line. Now draw the gap for the continuous curves, every composition of each phase model. Between the dots the SOLID curve dips below zero: at $x\approx0.4489$ it lies 61.2 J/mol atoms under the line, and the LIQUID curve 10.5 under it near 0.3197. The menu missed these states. How far a phase model's deepest point lies below the line is its driving force: minus the gap. It is the same idea as the gap between a curve and a reservoir's price line in [[boundary#where-the-odds-formula-comes-from|step 04]], which step 04 calls φ.
A negative gap is a state that would lower the energy if some of it formed: a positive driving force. Above the line means "not wanted at these prices"; on it means "can coexist".

The gap is the reduced cost $g_j-\pi_0-\pi_1x_j$, now over a continuum of columns. Complementary slackness: a dot strictly above the line is unused; a dot on the line may be used (or not). If the master's dual is unique, a negative reduced cost means the restricted master is not optimal for the full problem. At a degenerate master (z on a used dot at a kink of the envelope) the dual is not unique, and a dot can dip below the returned line although adding it does not lower the ceiling (step 15, rounds 1–2), or although the master is already optimal for the full problem (the [[lp-primer|LP primer]]'s short list at 0.65).

Moving the composition · Keep the menu and move $z$. For every $z$ strictly between 0.3 and 0.5 the same two dots are used, only their amounts change, and the line stays where it is. At $z=0.35$ the mixture is 0.75 LIQUID and 0.25 SOLID; at $z=0.45$ it is 0.25 and 0.75; the line, and so $\mu_A$ and $\mu_B$, is the same. The prices stay the same across the whole two-phase region. On this coarse menu the region runs from 0.3 to 0.5, wider than the true one from 0.312 to 0.441. Beyond it the used dots change: at $z=0.55$ the menu uses SOLID at 0.5 and SOLID at 0.7, two dots of the same phase model standing in for one solid.

blocks.label: Dive deeper · changing the temperature (about 5 min)

blocks.text: At other temperatures the curves move and the touching points move with them, tracing the lens of [[twophase/lab/part-c|part C of the step 03 lab]]: from liquid at 0.312 and solid at 0.441 at 1400 K towards the pure melting points, 1000 K for A and 1800 K for B. In optimisation words this is parametric cost analysis, while moving $z$ is a change of the right-hand side.

blocks.label: Dive deeper for operations research · ranging and support size (about 10 min)

blocks.text: The basis of LIQUID 0.3 and SOLID 0.5 stays optimal for $0.3\le z\le0.5$: right-hand-side ranging, with the duals fixed inside the range. A basic solution of two rows uses at most two states. That is related to, but not the same as, Gibbs' phase rule: grid states are not phases (two SOLID dots can stand for one solid), and one phase model can form two phases.
Approach · Use the gap table to decide which dots matter, then compute one gap of the continuous curve yourself, then move $z$ inside and outside the range.
Attempt · The line is $\mu_A=-19873.9$, $\Delta\mu=-1389.0$.

items: Which dots are used, and how can you tell from the gaps alone?
The continuous SOLID curve at $x=0.45$ has $g=-20560.14$. What is its gap? Should a state there be added?
At $z=0.45$, find the amounts of the two used dots. Does the line change?
At $z=0.55$ the menu uses SOLID 0.5 and SOLID 0.7. How many phases is that?

blocks.text: Two neighbouring dots of the same phase model stand for one phase whose composition lies between them.

LIQUID 0.3 and SOLID 0.5 have gap 0; all others are positive. At 0.45 the line is at $-20498.99$, so the SOLID gap is $-20560.14+20498.99=-61.15\approx-61.2$ J/mol atoms: negative, so a SOLID state near 0.45 would lower the energy. At $z=0.45$ the amounts are 0.25 LIQUID and 0.75 SOLID; the line does not change. At $z=0.55$ the two SOLID dots stand for one solid of composition between 0.5 and 0.7: one phase, two dots.

Explore · Open [[gap-curve/lab/gap|the gap-curve view]] and predict where the curves dip before you fade them in. Then [[gap-curve/lab/move-z|move z]] across and beyond 0.3 to 0.5, and [[gap-curve/lab/temperature|move the temperature]] to see the lens appear.

Interpret · The gap curve turns the whole problem into one picture. Everything at or above zero is fine at the current prices; anything below zero is a state the menu is missing. Its deepest point says which state to add next.
Think it over: the line is a floor for the menu, yet the curve dips below it. Is the line wrong?
Next · Step 13 adds the missing state and repeats.

modules.title: Column generation · find a missing state

blocks.text: In plain words: Your menu was too coarse. Instead of listing every state, ask: is anything below my line? The deepest dip of the gap curve answers that; add that state, redraw, repeat. Picture: the gap curve with its deepest dip marked.

Cards you may need: [[card#column-generation|column generation]], [[card#grid-sampling|what a grid can miss]], [[card#twin-dots|twin dots]], [[card#calphad-does-this|what CALPHAD codes do]], [[card#reduced-cost|reduced cost]].
Problem · What happens when you add the missing state to the menu, and when do you stop? The deepest dip of step 12 lies 61.2 J/mol atoms below the line, at SOLID $x\approx0.4489$.

Heads-up: model in steps 10–14: the melting lens of step 03 part C at 1400 K, a sample of overall B fraction $z=0.40$, phase models SOLID and LIQUID (A melts at 1000 K, this B at 1800 K). Energies are J/mol atoms.

Add the missing state · Solvers have three words for this loop: the menu problem is the master, the search for the deepest dip is pricing (which state is cheap at the current prices $\mu$?), and each added state is a column, one more column in the master's table of numbers. For these ideal curves the deepest dip has a formula: the gap curve's slope is zero there (the dive-deeper box "pricing in closed form" below writes it out); step 15 meets a curve where it has to be searched for. The new SOLID state has $x=0.44887$ and $g=-20558.60$ J/mol atoms. With it on the menu, the cheapest mixture at $z=0.40$ uses LIQUID at 0.3 and the new SOLID: by the lever rule, $f_{\mathrm{SOLID}}=0.1/0.14887=0.672$ and $f_{\mathrm{LIQUID}}=0.328$, at $-20470.64$ J/mol atoms. The ceiling dropped by 41.1. The line now passes through these two dots: $\Delta\mu=-1800.0$ and $\mu_A=-19750.7$.
With the new line, draw the gap curve again: there is a new deepest dip, now only 3.99 below, on the LIQUID side near 0.3121. Add it, solve, look again. Each round the dip is shallower:

After the first added state, two more additions bring the deepest dip to 0.0027 J/mol atoms; the used states approach the true compositions 0.312 and 0.441, and the line approaches the common tangent. Two neighbouring states of one phase model can share the amount of one phase for a while: twin dots, one phase. Stop when no state lies below the line by more than you care about. pycalphad does a version of this that prices only against its fixed grid of trial compositions.

This is a search for a missed state: ask the curves which composition, at the current prices, would lower the energy most. It is the same question as "which phase has the largest driving force?", answered for every composition at once.

A restricted master over the states found so far: its value is an upper bound, and adding the most negative reduced cost gives the Lagrangian lower bound of step 14. Pricing is solved exactly here, one column per round, and three columns close the bound to 0.0027 J/mol atoms. Notebook f4g reads the same loop as Kelley's cutting-plane method on the dual.

blocks.label: Dive deeper for operations research · pricing in closed form (about 10 min)

blocks.text: For an ideal phase model with end line $a+bx$, the gap is $a+bx+RT[x\ln x+(1-x)\ln(1-x)]-\mu_A-\Delta\mu\,x$. Its slope is $b-\Delta\mu+RT\ln\frac{x}{1-x}$, zero at $x^*=1/(1+e^{-(\Delta\mu-b)/RT})$, a logistic. For SOLID, $b=1000$; with $\Delta\mu=-1389.0$ and $RT=11640.3$ this gives $x^*=0.4489$. The gap is convex, so this stationary point is the global minimum: no search needed. The regular solution of step 15 is not convex, and that changes everything.

blocks.label: Dive deeper · where the effort goes in a CALPHAD program (about 10 min)

blocks.text: pycalphad 0.11.2 works in three stages: it samples states of every phase and solves the menu LP; a Newton-type solver then moves the compositions of the phases in use off the grid and returns new prices; then every sampled state is checked against the new line and the phase with the largest driving force is added, for up to ten rounds. With $C$ elements, a one-sublattice phase is sampled at $60(C-1)$ interior points by default (plus the pure ends and 60 points along each line between them: 122 for a binary phase): 60, 120, 240 and 540 for 2, 3, 5 and 10 elements, about 60, 11, 3.9 and 2.0 points per direction. The binary edges stay well covered; the inside of a many-element phase does not. The cost is mostly in evaluating energies at all those points, at every temperature; a valley between sparse points can be missed, and a denser grid costs more evaluations.

modules.title: Bounds · ceiling, floor and the remaining uncertainty

blocks.text: In plain words: Your best mixture says how high the answer can be at most. Slide the ruler down, keeping its tilt, until it touches the lowest point of the whole curve: nothing lies below that. The distance between the two is your remaining uncertainty in J/mol atoms. Picture: two marks on a number line, the truth between them.

Cards you may need: [[card#number-line|ceiling, floor, remaining uncertainty]], [[card#parallel-tangent|the parallel tangent]], [[card#floor-ceiling|floor and ceiling]], [[card#raw-grid-line|why the grid line is no floor]], [[card#tolerance|tolerance and −0.0]].
Problem · After any round of step 13, how far can the best mixture still be above the true minimum of the declared model?

Heads-up: model in steps 10–14: the melting lens of step 03 part C at 1400 K, a sample of overall B fraction $z=0.40$, phase models SOLID and LIQUID (A melts at 1000 K, this B at 1800 K). Energies are J/mol atoms.

Sliding the line down · The ceiling is the best real mixture found: the truth is at or below it, because a restricted calculation can only be higher, as with a solid-only calculation in step 01. For a floor, take the current line and slide it down, keeping its tilt, by the deepest dip of the whole gap curve. Now it lies under every state of both phase models, not just under the menu, and its height at $z$ is a floor for every possible mixture. This is the parallel tangent of step 07 or 09 used as a bound.

For the step 10 menu: ceiling $-20429.54$, deepest dip $-61.18$, floor $-20429.54-61.18=-20490.72$ J/mol atoms. The truth, $-20473.12$, lies between them, and the remaining uncertainty, ceiling minus the best floor found so far, is 61.2 (in optimisation words, the optimality gap). After column generation (round 3 of step 13) it is 0.0027 J/mol atoms. The floor is guaranteed here only because the deepest dip has a formula; a floor from a dip that might not be the deepest is no floor at all.

Scale: $RT$ at 1400 K is about 11.6 kJ/mol, and the parameters of a real assessment are typically uncertain by far more than 0.1 J/mol. The remaining uncertainty measures how well the declared model was solved, not how good the model is.
You met the parallel tangent in step 07 or 09 as a driving force. Here the same picture is a guarantee: once the line is slid below the whole curve, nothing can lie below it.

The floor is the Lagrangian bound of column generation with one convexity row: $\pi_0+\pi_1z+\min(0,\text{pricing minimum})=G_{\mathrm{up}}+\min(0,\text{dip})$. It is not monotone from round to round, so keep the best so far, and recompute the pricing minimum whenever the line changes. The raw line of a grid is not a bound for the continuous problem.

blocks.label: Dive deeper · finer menus instead of added states (about 5 min)

blocks.text: Instead of adding states, take finer menus with the sample never on a dot: spacing 0.2, 0.1, 0.02 and 0.002 give remaining uncertainties of 61.2, 52.0, 1.99 and 0.0095 J/mol atoms, using 5, 10, 50 and 500 dots per phase model. The menus are not nested, so a finer menu is not guaranteed to do better; what helps is a dot near the true compositions. Column generation got there with three added states.

blocks.label: Dive deeper for operations research · best-so-far and the bound that wobbles (about 5 min)

blocks.text: Here the raw floor happens to rise every round, but in general the Lagrangian bound can fall when the duals move. Report $\max$ over rounds of the raw bound, which stays valid because every raw bound is valid. The ceiling never rises, because the master keeps its columns.
Approach · For each round: the ceiling is the master's energy, the line is the master's line, and the floor is the line's height at $z$ minus the deepest dip.

Think it over: a colleague reports an equilibrium "to 0.0027 J/mol". What would you ask them before trusting that number?
Next · Step 15 switches to the regular solution, where the deepest dip can hide far from where you look.

modules.title: Global search · a local search can miss a valley

blocks.text: In plain words: A search that only looks near its starting point can report "single phase" while a deeper valley sits far away. A real supersaturated alloy may stay as it is for a long time, but an equilibrium calculation must find the deeper valley. Picture: the gap curve flat at 0.15, with a hidden dip near 0.96.

Cards you may need: [[card#which-model|which model this is]], [[card#local-global|local and global minimum]], [[card#metastable-unstable|metastable or unstable]], [[card#driving-force|driving force]], [[card#supersaturated|supersaturated solution and nucleus]].
Problem · Is the sample at $z=0.15$ a single phase? Start from the single state at 0.15 and its tangent: near 0.15 the gap curve shows no state below the line.

Heads-up: model in steps 15–17: the regular solution of step 03 part B at 800 K. One phase model, ALPHA: $g(x)=(1-x)(1000-10T)+x(13000-10T)+RT[x\ln x+(1-x)\ln(1-x)]+\Omega x(1-x)$ with $\Omega=20000$ J/mol and $R=8.3145$ J/(mol K): step 02's ALPHA with its own B plus a hump. The sample has $z=0.15$. This B is not the lens's B. Energies are J/mol atoms.

Local search can miss a valley · The tangent at 0.15 has slope $\Delta\mu=14462.1$ and touches the curve at $g(0.15)=-5461.7$, so $\mu_A=-7631.0$ J/mol atoms. Against this line the gap curve is zero at 0.15 and curves up on both sides: the curve bends up there, so the uniform state is stable against small changes. A search that walks downhill from 0.15 stays put; started at 0.05 it walks back to 0.15. Started anywhere from 0.3 upwards, it finds a valley the first search never saw: the full gap curve dips to $-2082.0$ J/mol atoms near $x=0.958$, where $g=4141.7$.

The sample at 0.15 is metastable, like the supersaturated solid of step 07 or 09. Physical metastability is real, but a calculation that promises equilibrium and returns the metastable state is wrong. If you want the metastable state, declare it as a restriction, here "the uniform state at 0.15 only", and solve that declared model. Suspending another phase would not do: one phase model can split into two phases by itself.

The dip marks the composition with the largest bulk driving force at the alloy's own chemical potentials: the parallel tangent. It is not the final equilibrium composition, and a real nucleus also depends on interface and elastic energy.

The gap curve against the tangent at the alloy's composition is the parallel-tangent picture of step 07 or 09: the deepest dip is the bulk driving force for precipitation. The calculation's job is to find it even when it is far away.

The pricing problem is now nonconvex: the gap curve has two local minima, so a local pricer can stop column generation too early. A one-state master leaves $\Delta\mu$ free; the tangent is our choice from local stationarity, not an LP output.

Keep pricing · Add the state at 0.958 and solve again. One added state is not enough: the solver's new line still lies above a deep part of the curve, so keep pricing. In rounds 1 and 2 the cheapest mixture is still the state at 0.15 alone: the sample sits on a used dot, so many lines touch the dots there (step 11), and the solver returns one of them, in round 1 a flat one. The deepest dip below that line still says which state to add, although the energy has not dropped yet. From round 3 added states on both sides of 0.15 form a split. Each round adds the deepest state of a full scan, and the used states move towards 0.070 and 0.930, the coexisting compositions of step 03 part B.

rows: the tangent at 0.15, chosen for illustration

blocks.label: Dive deeper for operations research · the degenerate master after one added state (about 10 min)

blocks.text: After adding the state at 0.958, no state lies left of $z=0.15$, so the only feasible mixture is the state at 0.15 itself. Every line through that dot that stays below the 0.958 dot is dual-optimal: $\Delta\mu\le$ about 11885 J/mol atoms. The tangent, with slope 14462, is not among them, which is why pricing against it found the 0.958 state. The solver returns one arbitrary member of that set, the flat line $\Delta\mu=0$, whose gap curve dips to $-1593.6$ near $x\approx0.009$. A hand-chosen line through the 0.15 and 0.958 dots would still dip $-132.7$ near 0.068. The dual you pick drives the next column: this is what dual stabilisation addresses in large problems; on this one-variable example it does not pay off (notebook f4g). Four more rounds after the flat line bring the dip below 0.01 J/mol atoms.
