Think it over: is a metastable alloy "wrong"? Is a calculation that returns it wrong? What is the difference?
Next · Step 16 checks that no valley deeper than a tolerance is left.

modules.title: Branch-and-bound · check that no valley is left

blocks.text: In plain words: Checking a curve point by point can never prove that no valley hides between the points. Cut the range into pieces and give each a cheap, guaranteed floor; cross out every piece that cannot go deeper than your tolerance and cut only the doubtful ones again. Picture: a row of interval bars, most crossed out.

Cards you may need: [[card#relaxation|relaxation and underestimator]], [[card#interval|intervals and halving]], [[card#prune-incumbent|prune and incumbent]], [[card#tolerance|tolerance]], [[card#checkable-answer|checkable answer]].

Problem · How do you check, without missing anything, that no state anywhere lies far below the final line? Column generation ended with the line through 0.070 and 0.930: $\mu_A=-7385.1$, $\Delta\mu=12000.0$, ceiling $-5585.11$ J/mol atoms, and two more rounds after those in step 15's table bring the deepest dip below 0.0001. Far means more than $\varepsilon=1$ J/mol atoms, anywhere on $[0,1]$.

Heads-up: model in steps 15–17: the regular solution of step 03 part B at 800 K. One phase model, ALPHA: $g(x)=(1-x)(1000-10T)+x(13000-10T)+RT[x\ln x+(1-x)\ln(1-x)]+\Omega x(1-x)$ with $\Omega=20000$ J/mol and $R=8.3145$ J/(mol K): step 02's ALPHA with its own B plus a hump. The sample has $z=0.15$. This B is not the lens's B. Energies are J/mol atoms.

A floor for a piece of the curve · The regular solution's curve is a straight line, plus the ideal mixing term (which bends up), plus the hump $\Omega x(1-x)$ (which bends down). On an interval $[l,u]$, replace the hump by its chord, the straight line joining its values at $l$ and $u$. An arch lies above its chord, so the new curve lies on or below the gap curve everywhere on the interval. And the new curve bends up everywhere, so its lowest point has a formula: where its slope is zero, $x^*=1/(1+e^{s/RT})$ with $s=b-\Delta\mu+\Omega(1-l-u)$ the slope of its straight parts ($b=13000-10T$ minus A's $1000-10T$, here 12000), clipped to $[l,u]$. Its value there is the interval's floor, guaranteed, with no search.

Prune or split · If an interval's floor is at least $-\varepsilon$, nothing in it lies deeper than the tolerance: cross it out (prune). Otherwise cut it in half and look at both halves. Start with $[0,1]$. The table follows the left half down to its smallest pieces; the right half mirrors it.

The intervals pile up near the touching points 0.070 and 0.930, where the line touches the curve and the floor can only beat $-\varepsilon$ on a short interval. After 27 intervals every piece of $[0,1]$ is pruned; the right half mirrors the left. Then no state lies more than the lowest floor $m$ of the pruned pieces below the line, and the floor for the sample is the line's height at $z$ lowered by $|m|$. That floor is never below the line lowered by $\varepsilon$.
If you stop early, some pieces of $[0,1]$ have never been examined: they have no floor at all. Only a computed floor can prune a piece.
The chord trick works for any curve whose awkward part is a hump: a bound you can draw. Near the touching points the intervals have to be short, because there the curve is close to the line.

A secant underestimator of the concave term and spatial branch-and-bound on one variable, used to solve the pricing problem globally. Branch-and-price is different: it branches on integer variables of the master, and nothing here is integer. The prune rule floor $\ge-\varepsilon$ proves only that the line lowered by $\varepsilon$ (or by the lowest leaf floor) is a floor, not the line itself.

blocks.label: Dive deeper for operations research · how short is short enough? (about 10 min)

blocks.text: The chord lies below the arch by at most $\Omega(u-l)^2/4$, at the midpoint. So near a touching point intervals must shrink to about $u-l\approx2\sqrt{\varepsilon/\Omega}\approx0.014$ before they can be pruned. That width is a scale, not a guarantee: at exactly that width the floor at a touching point is $-\varepsilon$ against the exact tangent, and $-1.005$ against a line 0.005 J/mol atoms too high, so the interval is split again. If the line's own gap dips to $-\delta$ ($\delta<\varepsilon$), pruning is guaranteed once $\Omega(u-l)^2/4<\varepsilon-\delta$. Here the halving reaches 1/128, about 0.0078.

blocks.label: Dive deeper · branch-and-bound as a search (about 5 min)

blocks.text: Run the same machinery against the tangent at 0.15 of step 15, keeping the deepest state found so far (the incumbent) and pruning every interval whose floor cannot beat it by more than 1 J/mol. After 15 intervals it has found the dip $-2082.0$ near 0.958 and checked that nothing is deeper by more than 1 J/mol: a pricing step that cannot miss a valley.

blocks.label: Dive deeper · a checkable answer (about 5 min)

blocks.text: The result can be checked without trusting the solver: the mixture (0.907 at 0.0701 and 0.093 at 0.9299), the line, and the 14 pruned intervals (of the 27 examined) that cover $[0,1]$. A short separate program recomputes every interval's floor from the formula, checks that no piece is missing and that ceiling minus floor is within 1 J/mol. It accepts this answer and rejects it if an interval is removed, if the line is raised by 2 J/mol, or if the floor is claimed 1 J/mol higher. In ordinary floating point this is a teaching check, not a rigorous proof.
Approach · Go through the table row by row: compare each floor with $-\varepsilon=-1$, then combine the pruned pieces into one floor.
Attempt · Use the table above and $\varepsilon=1$ J/mol atoms.

modules.title: Solved and good enough · the solver versus the model

blocks.text: In plain words: Two questions are easy to mix up. Did we solve the declared model? The advanced steps answered that with a ceiling, a floor and a check that no valley was left. Is the model good enough for the material? That needs data and judgement, not a better solver. Picture: two separate boxes, "solved?" and "good enough?".

Cards you may need: [[card#checkable-answer|checkable answer]], [[card#metastable-unstable|metastable or unstable]], [[card#driving-force|driving force]], [[card#calphad-database|CALPHAD and databases]], [[card#number-line|ceiling, floor, remaining uncertainty]].
Problem · Is the uniform state metastable or unstable, where is the bulk drive largest, and what is the equilibrium? Answer for two samples of the regular solution at 800 K: $z=0.15$ and $z=0.50$.

Heads-up: model in steps 15–17: the regular solution of step 03 part B at 800 K. One phase model, ALPHA: $g(x)=(1-x)(1000-10T)+x(13000-10T)+RT[x\ln x+(1-x)\ln(1-x)]+\Omega x(1-x)$ with $\Omega=20000$ J/mol and $R=8.3145$ J/(mol K): step 02's ALPHA with its own B plus a hump. The samples have $z=0.15$ and $z=0.50$. This B is not the lens's B. Energies are J/mol atoms.

Two questions · "Did we solve the declared model?" is answered by ceiling, floor and remaining uncertainty: 0.0027 J/mol atoms on the lens after column generation, 0.43 on the regular solution after branch-and-bound. "Is the model good enough?" is answered by data, parameters and predictions compared with experiments. A remaining uncertainty far below the model's own uncertainty is why both questions matter: a well-solved model can still be wrong. Equilibrium is the allowed state of lowest $G$ at fixed $T$ and $p$; whether and when a real sample reaches it is kinetics, which the second law does not decide.

blocks.label: Dive deeper · fit an elephant (about 20 min, with an optional notebook)

blocks.text: "With four parameters I can fit an elephant." Fit the miscibility gap of synthetic measurements with models of one to four parameters: calibrate on some temperatures, then predict the held-out ones. Which model fits the calibration data best, and which predicts best? The answer to "Is the model good enough?" comes from the second number, not the first.

What this does not tell you · The models are invented and no database here is validated. No method in these steps finds a phase that the model does not contain. A small energy difference does not guarantee the compositions. Interfaces and nuclei need their own description.
The joint case · Open the box for your background first, then the other one, and reconcile the two readings.

Operations-research card: from the printed outputs of steps 15 and 16, run column generation from the single state at 0.15 and state the bounds. Against the tangent at 0.50 (slope 12000.0), the gap curve has two dips of $-774.6$, at 0.070 and 0.930: what does a symmetric pricing result mean for the next column? (The two dips are equal because this model is symmetric about 0.5.)

The numbers: binodal 0.070 and 0.930, spinodal 0.211 and 0.789, curvature $+12.2$ kJ/mol atoms at 0.15 and $-13.4$ at 0.50; against the tangent at 0.50 (slope 12000.0) the gap curve dips to $-774.6$ at 0.070 and 0.930; against the tangent at 0.15 it dips to $-2082.0$ near 0.958.

Where is the bulk driving force largest, and how large is it?

blocks.text: Use the bending: up at 0.15, down at 0.50. Dips: $-2082.0$ near 0.958 against the tangent at 0.15; $-774.6$ at 0.070 and 0.930 against the tangent at 0.50.
Equilibrium: the lever rule on 0.070 and 0.930.

At $z=0.15$ the uniform state is metastable: the bulk drive is largest near 0.958, at 2082.0 J/mol atoms. The equilibrium is 0.070 and 0.930 with 0.907 and 0.093 of the sample, from column generation; branch-and-bound checks that the energy is within 0.43 J/mol atoms of the minimum (it does not pin down the compositions). At $z=0.50$ the curve bends down: unstable, it separates without a nucleation barrier. Because this model is symmetric about 0.5, the tangent at 0.50 has the same slope as the common tangent, so here the two equal dips at 0.070 and 0.930 happen to be the equilibrium compositions themselves, half each; in a model without that symmetry they would not be. The dip location is the composition of largest bulk drive, the dip depth is that drive, and the final compositions come from the converged calculation; a real critical nucleus also depends on interface and elastic energy.

Beyond materials · Column generation works the same way in cutting stock: columns are cutting patterns, the duals are prices of the ordered widths, and pricing finds the most profitable new pattern. Which operations-research problem do you know where the dual prices have a physical meaning, and what would a "driving force" be there? One lesson travels back: when the pricing problem is nonconvex, a local pricer can stop column generation too early, and a bound on the pricing problem is what lets you stop safely.

modules.title: Three components · menu, plane and tie line on a triangle

blocks.text: In plain words: Everything in steps 10–17 carries over to three components. The dots now sit on a triangle, the line becomes a tilted plane with three corner heights, and the gap becomes a landscape over the triangle. The same loop, add the state deepest below the plane, finds the split. Picture: a coloured triangle with one tie line across it.

Cards you may need: [[card#triangle|reading a triangle]], [[card#phase-rule|phase rule and tie line]], [[card#twin-dots|twin dots]], [[card#column-generation|column generation]], [[card#chemical-potential|chemical potential]].

Problem · Add a third component to the lens. Is the sample of composition $(0.50,0.30,0.20)$ solid, liquid or a split, and what are the compositions and amounts? Does the menu, the line and the gap curve still work?

Heads-up: this step is optional; no other step needs it. Model: the melting lens of steps 10–14 at 1400 K with an invented third component C, which melts at 1250 K (solid $1500-12T$, liquid $9000-18T$ J/mol). Both phase models stay ideal. The sample has $(z_A,z_B,z_C)=(0.50,0.30,0.20)$.

Points on a triangle · A composition now has three fractions that add to 1: a point in a triangle with A, B and C at its corners. The A–B side is the lens of steps 10–14, with its tie line from liquid at 0.312 to solid at 0.441 (in $x_B$). On the C–B side the tie line runs from 0.154 to 0.217 (in $x_B$). The A–C side is liquid everywhere at 1400 K, because both A and C melt below that.

The menu has three rows · Put dots on a triangular grid, every composition with steps of 1/12, for both phase models: 91 dots each. The master now keeps three balances: the amounts add to 1, the B atoms add to $z_B$, the C atoms add to $z_C$. Its cheapest mixture uses three dots: SOLID at $(0.417,0.417,0.167)$ with 0.3 of the sample, and two neighbouring LIQUID dots, $(0.500,0.250,0.250)$ with 0.4 and $(0.583,0.250,0.167)$ with 0.3, at $-25277.64$ J/mol atoms. Three positive amounts are not three phases: the two liquid dots are twins standing for one liquid between them, a small tie triangle approximating the tie line.

The line becomes a plane · The three multipliers give a plane over the triangle, with heights $\mu_A$, $\mu_B$ and $\mu_C$ at the corners: $-22733.0$, $-23222.0$ and $-34722.5$ J/mol for this menu. Its height at the sample is $0.5\mu_A+0.3\mu_B+0.2\mu_C=-25277.6$, the ceiling again. No menu dot lies below the plane.

The gap becomes a landscape · Subtract the plane from each phase model's energy everywhere on the triangle: a landscape, coloured by its height. Below-zero regions are states the menu is missing. For ideal phase models the deepest point still has a formula: each fraction is proportional to $e^{-(g^\circ_i-\mu_i)/RT}$.

Column generation on the triangle · Add the deepest state and solve again. The remaining uncertainty falls from 78.0 J/mol atoms on the menu to below 0.0001 in 15 rounds, and the used states close in on the split: liquid $(0.522,0.274,0.203)$, solid $(0.425,0.387,0.188)$, 0.771 of the sample liquid, at $-25345.11$ J/mol atoms. The tie triangle has collapsed onto a tie line through the sample.

This is a ternary isothermal section read as "which dots are used". The sample lies on its tie line, and the lever rule is read along it. Tie lines cannot be drawn with a ruler from the sample: they point neither to a corner nor parallel to a side, so a calculation is needed.

Three equality rows: a basic solution uses at most three states. Gibbs' phase rule at fixed $T$ and $p$ generically allows up to three coexisting phases, but this model has two phase models and no miscibility gap, so a third positive amount is a twin dot.

blocks.label: Dive deeper for operations research · an independent control: Rachford–Rice (about 10 min)

blocks.text: For two ideal phases the split follows from the partition ratios $K_i=x_{L,i}/x_{S,i}=e^{(g^\circ_{S,i}-g^\circ_{L,i})/RT}$: 1.229 for A, 0.709 for B and 1.080 for C. B prefers the solid, A and C the liquid. A split exists when $\sum_iz_iK_i>1$ and $\sum_iz_i/K_i>1$ (the Attempt asks you to check). The liquid amount $V$ then solves $\sum_iz_i(K_i-1)/(1+V(K_i-1))=0$, one monotone equation in one unknown on $0<V<1$: solve it for $V$ and compare with column generation's split.

blocks.label: Dive deeper · what gets harder (about 10 min)

items: The ideal ternary needs no global search: the gap landscape bends up everywhere, and its deepest point has a formula.

Give the liquid an A–C interaction, $\Omega=30000$ J/mol. Take the tangent plane at an A-rich liquid $(0.75,0.05,0.20)$: the landscape is zero there and rises nearby, but a full scan finds a hidden valley on the C-rich side near $(0.12,0.04,0.84)$, about 727 J/mol atoms deep. A local search from the tangent point never sees it.

Proving that no valley is left now needs floors on pieces of the triangle. The looseness of a chord-type bound shrinks like $\Omega h^2$ for pieces of size $h$, so $h\sim\sqrt{\varepsilon/\Omega}$, and a uniform grid of spacing $h$ has $\binom{1/h+d}{d}$ points on the composition simplex, roughly $(1/h)^d/d!$: about 100 for $h=0.01$ on a line, about 5000 on a triangle, about $4\times10^{12}$ for nine composition variables. That is the worst case: branch-and-bound refines only near the touching points and needs far fewer pieces (step 16), but each split of a piece in $d$ dimensions makes up to $2^d$ smaller ones and floors get weaker in more dimensions, so the cost still grows quickly.

blocks.text: Approach · Read the sample on the triangle, check the menu's answer with the three balances, read the plane at the sample, and check the split with the existence test. The test: for two ideal phases each component has a partition ratio $K_i=x_{\mathrm L,i}/x_{\mathrm S,i}$, fixed by its pure solid and liquid energies, here $K=(1.229,0.709,1.080)$; the sample splits exactly when both $\sum_iz_iK_i>1$ and $\sum_iz_i/K_i>1$.

With $K=(1.229,0.709,1.080)$, does the sample split? Compute $\sum z_iK_i$ and $\sum z_i/K_i$.

B atoms: $0.125+0.100+0.075=0.300$; C atoms: $0.050+0.100+0.050=0.200$. Two phases: one solid and one liquid, the liquid shown by two neighbouring dots.
